explanation: H⁺ ions from the acid combine with OH⁻ ions from the base to form water. Na⁺ and Cl⁻ stay dissolved as spectator ions, so the mixture ends up as ordinary salt water. Nothing changes colour and no gas is given off, but the tube becomes noticeably warm because the reaction releases heat.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — acids, bases and salts; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (standard enthalpy of neutralisation, about −57 kJ per mole)

hazard.title: Lead compounds are poisonous
hazard.warning: Both the lead(II) nitrate solution and the yellow lead(II) iodide formed are poisonous. Lead builds up in the body over time rather than being cleared out, so even small repeated exposures matter. It must never be touched with bare hands, tasted, or washed down the sink.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Handle lead solutions with gloves and wash your hands afterwards. Collect all lead waste in the labelled heavy-metal waste container so it can be disposed of properly instead of entering the water supply.

explanation: Two solutions that were both clear produce a bright yellow solid. Pb²⁺ ions from the lead nitrate meet I⁻ ions from the potassium iodide and join together as lead(II) iodide, which is insoluble in water and so drops out as a precipitate. K⁺ and NO₃⁻ take no part and stay dissolved as spectator ions. This is often demonstrated as the golden rain experiment.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — solubility rules and double displacement reactions; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (solubility of lead(II) iodide)

explanation: Ag⁺ ions from the silver nitrate meet Cl⁻ ions from the sodium chloride and form silver chloride, which is insoluble and appears as a white curdy precipitate. Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ remain in solution as spectator ions. This is the standard laboratory test for chloride ions. If the precipitate is left in sunlight it slowly darkens to grey or purple, because light breaks silver chloride down into silver metal.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — tests for anions and solubility rules; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (solubility and photosensitivity of silver chloride)

hazard.title: Flammable hydrogen gas is released
hazard.warning: The bubbles coming off the zinc are hydrogen, which burns very easily and forms an explosive mixture with the air. A naked flame brought near a large amount of collected hydrogen is dangerous.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Keep flames and hot surfaces away from the apparatus while gas is being given off, and work in a well ventilated room so the hydrogen can disperse.

explanation: Zinc sits above hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it can push hydrogen out of the acid. Each zinc atom gives up two electrons and enters the solution as a Zn²⁺ ion, while H⁺ ions from the acid pick up those electrons and pair off as hydrogen gas. You see a steady stream of bubbles on the surface of the metal and the tube warms up. The zinc slowly gets smaller as it dissolves. The pH shown assumes the acid is fully used up, leaving a zinc chloride solution that is still mildly acidic.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — reactivity series and reactions of metals with acids; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (standard enthalpy of formation data)

explanation: No observable change. The only products that could possibly form are sodium iodide and potassium chloride, and both of those are soluble in water. Since nothing insoluble can form, no precipitate appears, no gas is given off and the mixture stays clear and colourless. All four ions simply stay dissolved and move about independently. This is still a real chemical result and worth knowing: mixing two salt solutions does not automatically produce a reaction.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — solubility rules for common salts

explanation: Zinc is above copper in the reactivity series, so it takes the sulfate for itself and pushes the copper out. Each zinc atom gives up two electrons and enters the solution as Zn²⁺; the Cu²⁺ ions take those electrons and become copper metal, which settles on the zinc as a reddish-brown coating. The blue colour fades as the copper(II) ions leave the solution, which is the clearest sign the reaction is working. The mixture warms up because the reaction gives out heat.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, the reactivity series and displacement reactions

explanation: Iron is above copper in the reactivity series, so it displaces copper from the solution. The iron dissolves as Fe²⁺ ions and the copper comes out of solution as a reddish-brown coating on the iron. Here the colour change is between two colours rather than fading to nothing: the blue of copper(II) sulfate is replaced by the pale green of iron(II) sulfate. This is the reaction behind the old trick of an iron nail turning copper-coloured in blue vitriol.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, the reactivity series and displacement reactions

explanation: Magnesium is far above copper in the reactivity series, so this displacement is the most vigorous of the three. The blue colour disappears quickly, copper settles out as a dark reddish-brown powder, and the mixture becomes noticeably hot — much hotter than with zinc or iron. The bigger the gap between two metals in the reactivity series, the more energy the displacement gives out.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, the reactivity series and displacement reactions

hazard.title: Flammable hydrogen gas is released
hazard.warning: Magnesium reacts fast enough with acid to produce hydrogen in a hurry, and hydrogen forms an explosive mixture with air. The tube also becomes hot enough to be uncomfortable to hold.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Keep all flames well away while the metal is fizzing, use a small piece of ribbon rather than a long strip, and work in a well ventilated room so the hydrogen disperses.

explanation: Magnesium is high in the reactivity series, so it displaces hydrogen from the acid quickly. The metal gives up two electrons to become Mg²⁺, and the H⁺ ions from the acid take those electrons and pair up as hydrogen gas. You see a fast stream of bubbles, the ribbon shrinks and disappears, and the tube gets hot. Compare this with iron, which does the same thing far more slowly, and with copper, which cannot do it at all.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, reactions of metals with dilute acids

hazard.title: Flammable hydrogen gas is released
hazard.warning: The bubbles coming off the iron are hydrogen, which burns very easily and forms an explosive mixture with air.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Keep flames and hot surfaces away from the apparatus while gas is being given off, and work in a well ventilated room.

explanation: Iron is above hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it displaces hydrogen from dilute acid — but it sits much lower than magnesium, so the bubbling is slow and steady rather than vigorous. The solution turns pale green as iron(II) chloride forms. The difference in speed between magnesium, zinc and iron in the same acid is one of the clearest ways to see the reactivity series in action.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, reactions of metals with dilute acids

hazard.title: Flammable hydrogen gas, and the water turns strongly alkaline
hazard.warning: Calcium releases hydrogen steadily as it reacts, and hydrogen forms an explosive mixture with air. The calcium hydroxide left behind is strongly alkaline and attacks skin and eyes.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Keep flames away, add only a small granule of calcium at a time, and wear eye protection. Rinse any splashes off the skin with plenty of water.

explanation: Calcium is reactive enough to displace hydrogen from cold water, which magnesium cannot do. The granule sinks and fizzes steadily, giving off hydrogen, and the water becomes cloudy white because calcium hydroxide is only slightly soluble — the little that dissolves gives the strongly alkaline solution known as limewater, and the rest stays as a white suspension. Sodium and potassium do the same thing far more violently, which is why they are demonstrated only by a teacher.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, reactions of metals with water

hazard.title: Flammable hydrogen gas, and the apparatus is hot
hazard.warning: This reaction needs steam, so the apparatus is at boiling point throughout, and the hydrogen given off burns very easily.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Keep flames away from where the hydrogen escapes, and let the apparatus cool before handling it. Never seal the tube — trapped steam and gas must be able to escape.

explanation: Magnesium hardly touches cold water, but it reacts readily with steam. That is why nothing happens in this vessel until it is heated to about 100 °C. Once steam is present, the magnesium is oxidised to white magnesium oxide and hydrogen is driven off. The oxide is basic, so the little that dissolves leaves the water alkaline. This contrast — nothing in cold water, a clear reaction in steam — is exactly why the reactivity series has to be read alongside the conditions.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, reactions of metals with water and steam

explanation: No observable change. Copper sits BELOW hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it cannot push hydrogen out of the acid — no bubbles, no dissolving, no colour change, however long you wait. This is the single most useful "nothing happens" in the whole reactivity series: it is why copper is used for water pipes and roofing while iron rusts away, and it is the dividing line the series is really about. Zinc, iron and magnesium all sit above hydrogen and all fizz in this same acid.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, position of hydrogen in the reactivity series

explanation: No observable change. Copper is less reactive than zinc, so it cannot take the sulfate away from it — the copper stays as solid metal and the zinc stays in solution. Displacement only runs one way: a more reactive metal pushes out a less reactive one, never the other way round. Putting zinc into copper(II) sulfate gives a clear reaction; putting copper into zinc sulfate gives nothing at all.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, displacement runs only from more reactive to less reactive

explanation: No observable change. Zinc is below magnesium in the reactivity series, so it cannot displace magnesium from its salt. Compare this with zinc in copper(II) sulfate, where zinc is the more reactive metal and the reaction runs easily. Testing a metal against several different salt solutions, and noting which combinations do nothing, is exactly how the order of the reactivity series was worked out in the first place.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, establishing the order of the reactivity series

explanation: Every acid reacts with every carbonate in the same way: acid plus carbonate gives a salt, water and carbon dioxide. The carbonate ion takes two H⁺ ions from the acid to make carbonic acid, which is so unstable that it immediately falls apart into water and carbon dioxide — which is why you see fizzing rather than anything staying in solution. The gas that bubbles off turns limewater milky, and that is how you prove it is carbon dioxide.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Acids, Bases and Salts, reactions of acids with carbonates

explanation: Marble chips are calcium carbonate, and they fizz steadily in dilute hydrochloric acid, giving off carbon dioxide and slowly shrinking away. Because the chips are solid lumps the reaction proceeds at a rate you can watch and time, which is why this exact combination is the standard experiment for studying how surface area, concentration and temperature change the speed of a reaction. This is also the reaction that eats away limestone buildings in acid rain.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Acids, Bases and Salts, reactions of acids with carbonates

explanation: A hydrogencarbonate fizzes with acid just as a carbonate does, but it only needs one H⁺ per formula unit because it already carries one of its own hydrogens. The striking thing here is the temperature: the mixture gets COLDER, not hotter. Most acid–base reactions give out heat, so this is a rare and useful example of an endothermic reaction — one that takes heat in from its surroundings. That is why an instant cold pack can be made from much the same chemistry.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Acids, Bases and Salts, reactions of acids with hydrogencarbonates; Chemistry 9 — exothermic and endothermic changes

explanation: This is THE test for carbon dioxide. Limewater is a clear solution of calcium hydroxide; bubbling carbon dioxide through it produces calcium carbonate, which is almost insoluble, so it appears as a fine white solid that makes the clear liquid turn milky. Nothing else in ordinary school chemistry does this, which is what makes the test reliable. If you keep bubbling gas through for a long time the milkiness clears again, because excess carbon dioxide converts the carbonate into soluble calcium hydrogencarbonate.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Acids, Bases and Salts, the limewater test for carbon dioxide

explanation: A metal oxide is a base, so it neutralises an acid to give a salt and water — and nothing else. Black copper(II) oxide will not dissolve in water at all, but it dissolves readily in acid, and the colourless acid turns blue-green as copper(II) chloride forms. Notice there are no bubbles: that is the clearest way to tell a metal oxide from a carbonate, since a carbonate would fizz.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Acids, Bases and Salts, reactions of acids with metal oxides

explanation: Magnesium oxide is a basic oxide, so like copper(II) oxide it neutralises acid to a salt and water with no gas given off. The white powder simply disappears into the acid and the mixture warms up. Compare this with magnesium METAL in the same acid, which fizzes hydrogen off vigorously — the metal and its oxide behave quite differently, and telling them apart is a common examination question.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Acids, Bases and Salts, reactions of acids with metal oxides

explanation: Sulfuric acid is dibasic — each molecule gives away two H⁺ ions — so it takes two formula units of sodium hydroxide to neutralise one of acid, and the equation needs those coefficients to balance. Because twice as much water is being formed for each acid molecule, this releases noticeably more heat than the same amount of hydrochloric acid does. The salt left behind, sodium sulfate, is neutral, so the end point sits at pH 7.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Acids, Bases and Salts, neutralisation and basicity of acids

explanation: Nitric acid is monobasic, like hydrochloric acid, so one formula unit of alkali neutralises one of acid and the heat given out is close to that of the hydrochloric acid reaction. This is because in every neutralisation of a strong acid by a strong alkali the same thing is really happening: H⁺ and OH⁻ joining to make water. The sodium and nitrate ions are spectators, and evaporating the solution would leave sodium nitrate crystals behind.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Acids, Bases and Salts, neutralisation and preparation of salts

hazard.title: Flammable hydrogen gas is released
hazard.warning: The bubbles streaming off the zinc are hydrogen, which burns very easily and forms an explosive mixture with air.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Keep flames and hot surfaces well away while the metal is fizzing, and work in a well ventilated room so the hydrogen disperses.

explanation: Acid plus a metal above hydrogen in the reactivity series always gives a salt and hydrogen, whichever acid it is — only the salt changes. With hydrochloric acid zinc gives zinc chloride; with sulfuric acid the same metal gives zinc sulfate. This is the usual laboratory way of preparing hydrogen, and the gas is identified by the squeaky pop it makes with a lighted splint.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Acids, Bases and Salts, reactions of acids with metals; Chemistry 9 — preparation of hydrogen

hazard.title: Choking ammonia gas is released
hazard.warning: Ammonia has a sharp, choking smell and irritates the eyes, nose and throat. Warming the mixture drives it off quickly, and leaning over the tube to smell it directly is genuinely harmful.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Work in a fume cupboard or a well ventilated room, and never inhale directly over the tube. To identify the gas, hold damp red litmus paper at the mouth of the tube rather than putting your nose near it.

explanation: This is the standard test for an ammonium salt. Any alkali will displace ammonia from an ammonium compound, but the mixture has to be warmed before enough gas comes off to detect — which is why nothing much happens in this vessel until the burner is turned on. Ammonia is the only common alkaline gas, so damp red litmus paper turning blue at the mouth of the tube identifies it beyond doubt.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Acids, Bases and Salts, tests for ammonium salts

hazard.title: Soluble barium salts are poisonous
hazard.warning: The barium chloride solution used here is poisonous if swallowed. The barium sulfate it forms is harmless because it is so insoluble that the body cannot absorb it, but the solution it came from is not.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Handle barium solutions with care, wash your hands afterwards, and put the waste in the labelled heavy-metal container rather than down the sink.

explanation: This is the standard test for the sulfate ion. Barium sulfate is one of the most insoluble salts known, so the moment Ba²⁺ ions meet SO₄²⁻ ions a dense white precipitate appears. Sodium and chloride take no part and stay dissolved as spectator ions. In a real analysis the sample is acidified with hydrochloric acid first, so that a carbonate — which would also give a white precipitate — is destroyed before the barium chloride is added.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — tests for anions, the barium chloride test for sulfate

explanation: Silver nitrate is the standard reagent for identifying halide ions, and it tells the three apart by colour: a chloride gives a white precipitate, a bromide a cream one, and an iodide this distinct yellow. All three silver halides are insoluble, so the precipitate appears at once. Potassium and nitrate are spectator ions. Doing all three side by side is the only reliable way to judge the colours, because cream and white are hard to tell apart on their own.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — tests for anions, the silver nitrate test for halides

explanation: The middle member of the three halide tests. Silver bromide is cream — noticeably deeper than the white of silver chloride, but clearly paler than the yellow of silver iodide — and the colours deepen in that order going down Group 7. Silver bromide is extremely sensitive to light, and it was the compound coated onto photographic film for exactly that reason.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — tests for anions, the silver nitrate test for halides

explanation: Adding sodium hydroxide to a solution of a metal salt is the standard way of identifying the metal ion, because most metal hydroxides are insoluble and each has its own colour. Copper(II) gives this pale blue jelly-like precipitate, and no other common ion looks like it. The clear blue solution turning into a blue solid that will not settle quickly is the giveaway. Warming the precipitate turns it black as it loses water and becomes copper(II) oxide.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — tests for cations using sodium hydroxide

explanation: The test for the iron(II) ion. Sodium hydroxide precipitates a dull, dirty green solid quite unlike the clean colours of the other hydroxides. Left standing in air the surface slowly turns reddish brown, because oxygen converts iron(II) into iron(III) — which is the same change, and the same two colours, that you see when iron rusts.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — tests for cations using sodium hydroxide

explanation: The test for the iron(III) ion, and the one that makes the pair of iron tests worth doing together: iron(II) gives a dirty green precipitate and iron(III) this unmistakable reddish brown. Notice the equation needs three hydroxides rather than two, because the iron here carries a 3+ charge instead of 2+. What forms is essentially rust.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — tests for cations using sodium hydroxide

explanation: Magnesium gives a plain white precipitate with sodium hydroxide. Because several ions give white precipitates, a white result narrows the answer down rather than settling it — which is a useful lesson about qualitative analysis: one test rarely proves an identity on its own. The solid here is the same magnesium hydroxide sold as milk of magnesia for neutralising stomach acid.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — tests for cations using sodium hydroxide

explanation: A clean demonstration of a solubility rule: all sodium salts are soluble and all carbonates are insoluble EXCEPT those of Group 1 — so mixing a soluble calcium salt with a soluble carbonate must leave calcium carbonate behind as a solid. This is the same reaction that furs up kettles and pipes in hard-water areas, and the same white solid that makes limewater go milky.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — solubility rules and double displacement reactions

hazard.title: Lead compounds are poisonous
hazard.warning: Both the lead(II) nitrate solution and the white lead(II) chloride formed are poisonous. Lead builds up in the body rather than being cleared out, so even small repeated exposures matter.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Handle lead solutions with gloves and wash your hands afterwards. Collect all lead waste in the labelled heavy-metal container rather than washing it down the sink.

explanation: The solubility rule for chlorides is that they are all soluble EXCEPT silver, lead and mercury(I) — and this is that exception in action. Lead(II) chloride is unusual among precipitates because it is only slightly insoluble: warming the tube dissolves it again, and on cooling it comes back as glittering white needles. That reversibility is a good reminder that solubility depends on temperature.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — solubility rules for chlorides and their exceptions

explanation: No observable change. Work out what could possibly form: copper(II) chloride and sodium sulfate. Check both against the solubility rules — all common chlorides except silver, lead and mercury(I) are soluble, and all sodium salts are soluble — so neither product can leave the solution, and nothing precipitates. The blue simply stays blue. This is the routine you should follow before every double displacement: name the two possible products, look both up, and only expect a precipitate if one of them is insoluble.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — applying solubility rules to predict double displacement reactions

hazard.title: Burning magnesium gives off blinding ultraviolet light
hazard.warning: Magnesium burns with an intensely bright white flame that contains a lot of ultraviolet. Looking straight at it can damage the eyes, and the flame is hot enough to set light to anything nearby. Water must never be used on a magnesium fire — it makes it worse, because magnesium reacts with steam.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Look at the flame indirectly or through darkened glass, never straight at it. Burn only a short piece held in tongs over a heatproof mat, and smother a magnesium fire with dry sand rather than water.

explanation: Oxidation in its oldest and simplest sense: a substance gaining oxygen. Each magnesium atom loses two electrons to an oxygen atom, so magnesium is oxidised and oxygen is reduced — the two always happen together, which is why these are called redox reactions. The white ash left behind is magnesium oxide, and it weighs MORE than the magnesium you started with, because the oxygen has been added to it.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Electrochemistry, oxidation and reduction; Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, reactions of metals with oxygen

explanation: Copper is unreactive enough that it will not touch oxygen at room temperature — this is why copper roofs and pipes last so long. Heat it strongly, though, and the surface turns from reddish brown to black as copper(II) oxide forms. The colour change is easy to reverse: passing hydrogen over the hot black oxide turns it back to bright copper, which is the standard demonstration of reduction.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Electrochemistry, oxidation as gain of oxygen

hazard.title: Hydrogen and a hot tube together
hazard.warning: Hydrogen forms an explosive mixture with air, and this reaction needs the tube to be hot. Air left in the apparatus when the hydrogen is lit is what makes this dangerous rather than the reaction itself.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Let the hydrogen flow long enough to sweep all the air out of the apparatus before heating, and keep heating until the flow is stopped so no air is drawn back in.

explanation: The mirror image of the reaction above, and the classic demonstration of reduction: the black copper(II) oxide LOSES its oxygen and turns back into bright reddish-brown copper, while the hydrogen GAINS that oxygen and leaves as water. Both halves happen at once — copper oxide is reduced, hydrogen is oxidised. Here hydrogen is acting as the reducing agent, which is exactly the job carbon monoxide does in a blast furnace when iron is extracted from its ore.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Electrochemistry, reduction as loss of oxygen and the action of reducing agents

explanation: Halogen displacement is redox seen through electrons rather than oxygen. Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it takes the electrons: each chlorine atom gains an electron to become a chloride ion (chlorine is reduced), while each bromide ion loses one to become bromine (the bromide is oxidised). You can follow it by colour alone — a nearly colourless mixture turns orange-brown as bromine appears.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, reactivity of the halogens; Electrochemistry, redox as electron transfer

explanation: Chlorine is more reactive than iodine as well, so it displaces it just as it displaced bromine — and the colour change is even more striking, from almost colourless to a deep brown as iodine forms. Because chlorine displaces both of the others, and neither of them can displace chlorine, chlorine must be the most reactive of the three.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, reactivity of the halogens

explanation: The middle step that settles the order. Bromine cannot displace chlorine, but it CAN displace iodine — the orange-brown of bromine deepens to the brown of iodine. Put together with the two chlorine reactions, this fixes the Group 7 order beyond doubt: chlorine, then bromine, then iodine, with reactivity falling as you go down the group.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, reactivity of the halogens

explanation: No observable change. Iodine is BELOW bromine in Group 7, so it is the less reactive of the two and cannot take the electrons away from bromide ions. The brown of the iodine simply stays as it was. This negative result is what makes the other three trustworthy: displacement works in one direction only, and finding the direction that fails is how the order of reactivity is proved rather than assumed.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, establishing the order of halogen reactivity

explanation: Rusting is the slow oxidation of iron, and it needs BOTH oxygen and water — leave either one out and it does not happen, which is what the two entries alongside this one show. The iron loses electrons to oxygen, so the iron is oxidised. What makes rust so destructive compared with the oxide layer on aluminium is that it flakes off instead of sealing the surface, so fresh iron keeps being exposed. Painting, greasing, galvanising and sacrificial protection all work by keeping oxygen and water away from the metal, or by giving them something more reactive to attack instead.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Electrochemistry, corrosion of iron and methods of its prevention

explanation: No observable change. Iron sitting in dry oxygen does not rust, however long it is left. This is one half of the classic three-tube experiment: iron in air and water rusts, iron in dry air does not, and iron in water with the air boiled out does not either. Both must be present together. It is also why tools kept in a dry store stay bright while the same tools left outside go orange within days.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Electrochemistry, conditions necessary for rusting

explanation: No observable change. Iron under water that has had the air boiled out of it does not rust, because although water is present there is no oxygen for the iron to lose its electrons to. This is the other half of the three-tube experiment, and the pair of negative results together prove something a single positive result never could: that rusting needs oxygen AND water, not just one or the other.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Electrochemistry, conditions necessary for rusting

cathode.observation: Twice as much gas collects here as at the anode.

anode.observation: Half as much gas as at the cathode, and it relights a glowing splint.

hazard.title: Hydrogen and oxygen are being made together
hazard.warning: Electrolysing water produces hydrogen and oxygen in exactly the proportions that burn most fiercely. Collected together in one container they form an explosive mixture, and a flame or spark is all it takes.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Collect the two gases in separate tubes, one over each electrode, and keep all flames away until you are ready to test each gas on its own.

explanation: Water is split into its two elements by an electric current. Positive hydrogen ions drift to the negative electrode (the cathode) where they collect electrons and leave as hydrogen gas; negative hydroxide ions drift to the positive electrode (the anode) where they give electrons up and leave as oxygen. Exactly twice as much hydrogen is produced as oxygen, which matches the formula H₂O and is the easiest way to see that formula being confirmed by experiment. In practice a few drops of dilute sulfuric acid are added first, because pure water conducts far too poorly on its own — the acid is not used up.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Electrochemistry, electrolysis of water

cathode.observation: Hydrogen, not sodium — the water is discharged in preference to the more reactive metal.

anode.observation: Choking pale green chlorine, which bleaches damp litmus paper.

hazard.title: Poisonous chlorine gas is released
hazard.warning: Chlorine given off at the anode is poisonous to breathe and attacks the eyes and lungs. It is denser than air, so it collects low down rather than dispersing upwards. Hydrogen is coming off the other electrode at the same time, and that is flammable.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Run this only in a fume cupboard or a very well ventilated room, and never lean over the cell. Keep flames away from the cathode side because of the hydrogen.

explanation: Electrolysing concentrated salt solution — brine — gives three useful products at once, which is why it is one of the biggest chemical industries in the world. Chloride ions go to the anode and leave as chlorine gas. At the cathode it is NOT sodium that appears, even though sodium ions are drifting there: sodium is too reactive to be discharged out of water, so hydrogen ions from the water take the electrons instead and hydrogen bubbles off. That leaves sodium and hydroxide ions behind in the cell, so the solution turns strongly alkaline.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Electrochemistry, electrolysis of brine and the Nelson cell

cathode.observation: Molten silvery sodium collects here and floats on the melt.

hazard.title: Molten salt at 800 °C, poisonous chlorine, and sodium metal
hazard.warning: This cell runs at over 800 °C. The chlorine given off is poisonous, and the sodium produced catches fire in air and reacts violently with water. All three hazards are present at once, which is why this is an industrial process and not a school experiment.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: This is shown here as a simulation of the industrial Down's cell. It is not something to attempt in a school laboratory at all — study the diagram and the half equations instead.

explanation: Solid salt does not conduct, because its ions are locked in the crystal and cannot move — which is why this vessel does nothing until it is heated past the melting point of about 801 °C. Once molten, the ions are free, and now the current can pull them apart: sodium ions to the cathode where they become sodium metal, chloride ions to the anode where they become chlorine gas. With no water present there is nothing to be discharged in preference, so this time the sodium really does appear. This is the only practical way to obtain such a reactive metal, and it is how the industrial Down's cell works.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Electrochemistry, electrolysis of molten sodium chloride and the Down's cell

effects.precipitate: reddish brown copper on the cathode

cathode.observation: A reddish-brown layer of copper plates onto the electrode, and the blue fades from the solution.

anode.observation: Oxygen bubbles off, because sulfate ions are not discharged.

explanation: This is the reaction behind electroplating and behind the refining of copper. Copper(II) ions are pulled to the cathode, where they collect electrons and stick to it as a solid layer of copper — so whatever object you make the cathode gets copper-plated. Because the copper is being taken out of the solution, the blue colour fades as the reaction goes on, which makes progress easy to watch. At the anode the sulfate ion is too stable to be discharged, so hydroxide ions from the water give up their electrons instead and oxygen bubbles off, leaving the solution increasingly acidic.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Electrochemistry, electrolysis of copper(II) sulfate, electroplating and refining

hazard.title: Choking sulfur dioxide is produced
hazard.warning: Sulfur dioxide has a sharp, choking smell and irritates the eyes, nose and lungs. It is the gas that makes acid rain, and breathing it is genuinely harmful — people with asthma react to it badly.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Burn sulfur only in a fume cupboard, and use the smallest amount that shows the effect. Never lean over the burning sulfur to smell the gas directly.

explanation: Sulfur burns in air with a striking blue flame to give sulfur dioxide. It matters far beyond the laboratory: coal and oil contain sulfur as an impurity, so burning them in a power station does exactly this on an enormous scale, and the sulfur dioxide released is the main cause of acid rain. Removing sulfur from fuels before burning them, and scrubbing it out of chimney gases afterwards, are the two ways of preventing it.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — The Atmosphere, air pollutants and their sources

explanation: This is acid rain being made, in one step. Sulfur dioxide from burning fuel dissolves in the water of a cloud droplet and turns it into sulfurous acid. Dip pH paper in before and after and the change is dramatic — from neutral water to a strongly acidic solution. Rain like this dissolves limestone buildings and statues, strips nutrients out of soil, and kills fish by acidifying lakes. In the atmosphere it is oxidised further to sulfuric acid, which is stronger still.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — The Atmosphere, acid rain and its effects

explanation: Carbon burning in plenty of air glows red and gives carbon dioxide. The words IN PLENTY OF AIR matter: where the air supply is restricted the same carbon burns to carbon monoxide instead, a colourless and odourless gas that stops blood carrying oxygen and kills people in rooms with badly ventilated heaters. Same fuel, same element, and the only difference is how much oxygen reaches it. Carbon dioxide itself is not poisonous, but it is the main greenhouse gas driving climate change.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — The Atmosphere, complete and incomplete combustion

explanation: Carbon dioxide dissolves in water to make carbonic acid, a very weak acid. This is why perfectly clean, unpolluted rain is already slightly acidic at about pH 5.6 — so acid rain does not mean rain that is acidic, it means rain MORE acidic than that natural background. It is also the reaction that puts the sharpness into fizzy drinks, and, working over thousands of years, the one that dissolves limestone into caves.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — The Atmosphere, natural acidity of rainwater

explanation: Nitrogen and oxygen sit mixed together in every breath of air and do absolutely nothing, because the triple bond holding N₂ together is one of the strongest in chemistry. Only at about 1500 °C and above — the temperature inside a lightning bolt or a car engine — is there enough energy to break it. That is why this vessel does nothing until it is extremely hot. The reaction also ABSORBS energy rather than releasing it, which is the other reason it needs such extreme conditions.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — The Atmosphere, oxides of nitrogen and their formation

hazard.title: Poisonous brown nitrogen dioxide forms
hazard.warning: Nitrogen dioxide is poisonous and attacks the lungs, and unlike many hazards it gives little warning — the damage can appear hours after breathing it.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Keep oxides of nitrogen in a fume cupboard and never smell them directly. The brown colour alone is enough to identify the gas.

explanation: This one is worth watching rather than reading about: a colourless gas turns brown the instant it meets air. Nitrogen monoxide from an engine does exactly this as soon as it leaves the exhaust, and that brown haze hanging over a congested city on a still day is largely nitrogen dioxide. It is also the step that turns a fairly harmless gas into a poisonous one and into a cause of acid rain.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — The Atmosphere, oxides of nitrogen

explanation: The second route to acid rain. Nitrogen dioxide dissolves in cloud droplets, along with oxygen from the air, to give nitric acid — and the brown colour disappears as it goes into solution. Between them, sulfur dioxide from burning coal and nitrogen oxides from engines account for nearly all acid rain. Note that the acid in real rain is enormously more dilute than anything in a bottle on the shelf; it is the sheer volume falling year after year that does the damage.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — The Atmosphere, acid rain from oxides of nitrogen

explanation: This is why the hardness is called TEMPORARY: boiling alone destroys it. Calcium hydrogencarbonate is only stable while it is cold and dissolved, so heating breaks it apart into insoluble calcium carbonate, water and carbon dioxide. The calcium that made the water hard leaves the solution as a white solid — which is the limescale that furs up kettles, blocks hot water pipes and coats heating elements. Notice that the vessel does nothing until it actually reaches 100 °C.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Water, removal of temporary hardness by boiling

explanation: Clark's method: temporary hardness can be removed cold, without boiling, by adding just the right amount of limewater. It looks strange at first — adding more calcium to get rid of calcium — but it works because the hydroxide converts the soluble hydrogencarbonate into insoluble carbonate, and BOTH lots of calcium come out together as a solid. Adding too much limewater simply makes the water alkaline instead, so the amount has to be calculated rather than guessed. Boiling a whole town's water supply is impossible; this is cheap enough to do at scale.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Water, Clark's method for removing temporary hardness

explanation: Permanent hardness is the kind boiling cannot touch, so it has to be dealt with chemically. Washing soda supplies carbonate ions, which grab the calcium out of solution as insoluble calcium carbonate and leave harmless sodium sulfate behind. With the calcium gone the water lathers properly instead of forming scum, which is exactly why washing soda has been added to laundry for generations. Compare this with boiling, which does nothing at all to permanent hardness.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Water, removal of permanent hardness using washing soda

explanation: The clearest demonstration there is of what a catalyst does. Hydrogen peroxide decomposes on its own, but so slowly that a bottle keeps for months. Drop in a little black manganese(IV) oxide and it foams vigorously at once. The catalyst provides an easier route for the same reaction — a lower activation energy — so far more collisions succeed. It is not used up: filter it out at the end, dry it, weigh it, and you have exactly what you started with, ready to do it again. Note it is the reaction that warms the flask, not the catalyst.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Reaction Kinetics, catalysis and activation energy; Chemistry 9 — preparation of oxygen

hazard.title: A strong oxidiser being heated
hazard.warning: Potassium chlorate gives up oxygen readily when hot. Mixed with anything that burns — paper, sulfur, a trace of organic dust in the tube — it can ignite the mixture fiercely or explosively.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Heat it only in a scrupulously clean, dry tube, never grind it with anything combustible, and use small amounts. Add the catalyst rather than a hotter flame if it is slow.

explanation: The other standard laboratory preparation of oxygen, and a second look at catalysis from a different angle. Potassium chlorate heated on its own needs a fierce flame before it gives up its oxygen; mixed with a little manganese(IV) oxide it does the same job at a much lower temperature. The catalyst has not changed WHAT happens or how much oxygen you get — only how easily it happens. Test the gas with a glowing splint: it should burst back into flame.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Reaction Kinetics, effect of a catalyst; preparation of oxygen

explanation: The Haber process, which takes nitrogen straight from the air and turns it into the ammonia that becomes fertiliser — the reason the world can feed as many people as it does. Industrially it runs at about 450 °C and 200 atmospheres over an iron catalyst. Those numbers are a compromise, and that is the lesson: the reaction gives out heat, so a LOW temperature would favour more ammonia at equilibrium, but a low temperature is also unbearably slow. 450 °C is chosen not because it gives the best yield but because it gives a workable yield quickly. High pressure genuinely does favour ammonia, because four molecules of gas become two. This lab does not model pressure, so treat the vessel here as showing the chemistry rather than the yield.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Chemical Equilibrium, Le Chatelier's principle and the Haber process

explanation: The heart of the Contact process, the way almost all the world's sulfuric acid is made. Sulfur dioxide and oxygen are passed over vanadium(V) oxide at about 450 °C. The same compromise as the Haber process applies — the reaction is exothermic, so cooler would mean a better yield but an unusably slow one. The catalyst works by handing oxygen back and forth: it is reduced by the sulfur dioxide and then re-oxidised by the oxygen, over and over, ending each cycle exactly as it began.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Industrial Chemistry, the Contact process

hazard.title: A violent reaction that throws off a mist of acid
hazard.warning: Sulfur trioxide meeting water reacts so fiercely, and gives out so much heat, that much of the acid is thrown up as a choking mist of fine droplets rather than staying in the vessel. That mist is concentrated sulfuric acid and attacks the eyes and lungs.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: This is why industry never does it this way. The sulfur trioxide is absorbed into concentrated sulfuric acid first, giving oleum, and the oleum is then diluted with water under control.

explanation: The last step of the Contact process, and a good example of a reaction that is simple to write and awkward to carry out. On paper sulfur trioxide plus water gives sulfuric acid. In practice it is so violently exothermic that it produces an unmanageable acid mist, so the plant dissolves the sulfur trioxide in concentrated sulfuric acid to make oleum and dilutes that instead. Same overall change, arrived at safely — a reminder that an equation says what happens, not how to do it.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Industrial Chemistry, the Contact process and oleum

explanation: The first stage of the Ostwald process, which turns the ammonia from the Haber process into nitric acid. Ammonia and air are passed over a platinum gauze at about 900 °C; the reaction gives out so much heat that once it starts the gauze glows and stays hot without further heating. The nitrogen monoxide made here goes on to react with more oxygen to give nitrogen dioxide, and that with water to give nitric acid — the same two steps that happen accidentally in polluted air and produce acid rain.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Industrial Chemistry, the Ostwald process

hazard.title: Hydrogen and oxygen together are explosive
hazard.warning: Hydrogen mixed with oxygen or air burns explosively the instant it is lit. A test tube of the mixture gives the sharp squeaky pop used to identify hydrogen; a larger volume is genuinely dangerous.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Test only a small tube of gas at a time, hold it away from your face, and never light a large collected volume. Point the mouth of the tube away from anyone before applying a flame.

explanation: The squeaky pop test, and the reaction that identifies hydrogen. It is worth noticing what the product is: burning hydrogen makes nothing but water, no carbon dioxide and no smoke at all, which is why hydrogen is of such interest as a fuel. The catch is that hydrogen has to be made first, and today most of it is made from natural gas in a process that releases carbon dioxide — so the fuel is only as clean as the way it was produced.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — properties of hydrogen and its test; Chemistry XI — Thermochemistry

explanation: Two colourless things meet and produce a dense white smoke out of apparently nothing — which is why this is a demonstration people remember. The smoke is a cloud of tiny solid ammonium chloride particles. It is also an acid–base reaction with no water involved anywhere: the ammonia takes a hydrogen ion directly from the hydrogen chloride. That is exactly the case the Arrhenius definition of an acid cannot describe and the Brønsted–Lowry definition can, which is the main reason the definition had to be widened.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Acids and bases, the Brønsted–Lowry definition

explanation: Ammonia is extraordinarily soluble in water — so soluble that the classic fountain experiment works, where water rushes up into a flask of the gas as it dissolves and the pressure drops. What forms is a WEAK base: at any moment only a small fraction of the ammonia has actually taken a hydrogen ion from the water, and the double arrow says so. Compare the pH here, 11.5, with sodium hydroxide's 14 at a similar concentration. That gap is the difference between weak and strong, and it has nothing to do with being dilute or concentrated.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Acids and bases, strong and weak bases

explanation: Heating baking soda turns it into washing soda, driving off water and carbon dioxide. This is the reaction that makes a cake rise: the carbon dioxide released inside the batter is what lifts it, and the residue left behind is harmless. Industrially it is the last step of the Solvay process, which manufactures sodium carbonate from salt and limestone. Test the gas with limewater — turning milky confirms carbon dioxide.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Industrial Chemistry, the Solvay process; thermal decomposition of hydrogencarbonates

effects.dissolves: the white crystals disappeared into the water

explanation: An ENDOTHERMIC change, and one you can feel. Dissolving takes two steps: pulling the ions out of the crystal costs energy, and letting water molecules cluster round them releases it. For ammonium nitrate the first costs more than the second gives back, so the difference is taken from the surroundings and the beaker turns genuinely cold to hold. This is exactly what is inside an instant cold pack — squeeze it, the inner bag of water breaks, and the injury gets cooled with no freezer anywhere. It is also the clearest possible answer to the idea that reactions always give out heat.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Thermochemistry, enthalpy of solution; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (enthalpy of solution +25.7 kJ/mol)

effects.dissolves: the white crystals disappeared into the water

explanation: Also endothermic, but less sharply so than ammonium nitrate — put the two side by side and the difference in how cold each beaker gets is the enthalpy of solution being measured by hand. Potassium nitrate is also the salt to use for showing solubility against temperature: very much more of it dissolves in hot water than cold, so a hot saturated solution left to cool grows crystals as it goes.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Thermochemistry and Solutions, enthalpy of solution and solubility curves; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (enthalpy of solution +34.9 kJ/mol)

effects.dissolves: the white crystals disappeared into the water

explanation: The mildest of the three endothermic dissolutions here, cooling the water by a few degrees. Having three of them at different strengths is the point: the enthalpy of solution is a property of the particular salt, not something that all dissolving does. The solution left is acidic, because the ammonium ion gives a hydrogen ion back to the water.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Thermochemistry, enthalpy of solution; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (enthalpy of solution +14.8 kJ/mol)

effects.dissolves: the white lumps disappeared into the water

explanation: The same two steps as ammonium nitrate, coming out the other way round. Calcium chloride's ions are small and doubly charged, so water molecules cluster round them very tightly and release more energy than it cost to break the crystal apart — the beaker gets hot. This is the chemistry inside a reusable hand warmer, and it is also why bags of calcium chloride are spread on icy roads.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Thermochemistry, enthalpy of solution and hydration; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (enthalpy of solution −81.3 kJ/mol)

effects.dissolves: the white pellets disappeared into the water

hazard.title: A corrosive solid dissolving, and getting hot doing it
hazard.warning: Sodium hydroxide attacks skin and eyes, and dissolving it releases enough heat that a strong solution can become hot enough to spit. Both hazards arrive at once.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Add the pellets to plenty of water a few at a time, never water to the pellets, and stir as you go so the heat spreads out. Wear eye protection throughout.

explanation: Strongly exothermic — dissolving sodium hydroxide in only a little water can drive it close to boiling. Notice this is dissolving, not neutralising: no acid is involved and no new substance is made, yet a great deal of heat comes out. That is worth separating from the enthalpy of neutralisation, which is a different quantity measured for a different change and often confused with it.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Thermochemistry, enthalpy of solution; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (enthalpy of solution −44.5 kJ/mol)

hazard.title: Slaking lime is violent and the water can boil
hazard.warning: Quicklime reacts with water so vigorously that the lump cracks and hisses, steam comes off it, and the water can reach boiling point with no burner anywhere near. The calcium hydroxide formed is strongly alkaline and attacks eyes badly. Quicklime in a damp eye reacts with the moisture there.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Add a small lump to plenty of cold water, never the other way round, stand back, and wear eye protection. Never handle quicklime with damp hands.

explanation: Slaking, and about the most violently exothermic thing a school laboratory demonstrates without setting light to anything. The lump swells, cracks and steams, and a thermometer in the water climbs dozens of degrees on its own. It is the middle step of the lime cycle that has been used in building for thousands of years: roast limestone to quicklime, slake it to make lime putty, and the putty then slowly absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and hardens back into limestone.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Thermochemistry, exothermic reactions; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (enthalpy of reaction −63.7 kJ/mol)

explanation: The standard chemical test for water. White anhydrous copper(II) sulfate turns blue the instant water touches it, and gets warm doing so, because the water is being locked into the crystal structure itself — water of crystallisation. Be careful what the test proves: it says water is PRESENT, not that the liquid is pure water. Tap water, sea water and orange juice all turn it blue. Proving something is pure water needs a boiling point of 100 °C and a freezing point of 0 °C as well.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Water, chemical test for water; Chemistry XI — water of crystallisation

explanation: Heating the blue crystals drives the water of crystallisation out of them and the colour drains away to white. The water does not vanish — it condenses on the cool upper part of the tube, where you can see it and test it. This is endothermic: it takes energy to pull that water out, which is why it needs a burner. Add water to the white powder afterwards and the blue comes straight back, which is what makes this pair the clearest demonstration of a hydrate there is.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — water of crystallisation and its removal by heating

explanation: The other test for water, and the one that comes on paper. Filter paper soaked in cobalt(II) chloride and dried is blue; touch it with water and it turns pink at once. It is more convenient than the copper sulfate test because the paper can be dried and used again, and because blue to pink is easier to judge at a glance than white to blue. Both tests answer the same limited question: is there water here, not is this pure water.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Water, cobalt chloride test for water

explanation: Warming the pink hydrate drives its six waters off and it returns to blue — which is why cobalt chloride paper is reusable in a way copper sulfate is not. Put the two hydrate pairs side by side and the general rule appears: a hydrate's colour belongs to the water built into its crystal, and heating takes the water and the colour away together.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — water of crystallisation; Chemistry 10 — cobalt chloride paper

explanation: The silver tree, and one of the most beautiful demonstrations in chemistry: leave a coil of copper wire in silver nitrate and needles of silver grow out of it over an hour while the solution turns blue. Copper's electrode potential is +0.34 V and silver's is +0.80 V, so the cell voltage for this change is 0.80 − 0.34 = +0.46 V. A POSITIVE cell voltage is what says a redox reaction will go on its own, and this is the number the electrochemical series exists to let you look up. The blue appearing is the copper going into solution; the needles are the silver coming out of it.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Electrochemistry, electrochemical series and cell potential; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (standard electrode potentials)

explanation: The same silver tree, grown from zinc instead of copper — and it happens faster and gives out more heat. The reason is in the numbers: zinc is at −0.76 V, so the cell voltage here is 0.80 − (−0.76) = +1.56 V, more than three times the copper figure. The further apart two metals sit in the electrochemical series, the larger the voltage and the more vigorous the displacement. Comparing these two reactions side by side is how that relationship stops being a table to memorise and becomes something you can watch.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Electrochemistry, electrochemical series and cell potential; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (standard electrode potentials)

explanation: No observable change, and the electrochemical series says why before you try it. Silver is at +0.80 V and copper at +0.34 V, so this way round the cell voltage is 0.34 − 0.80 = −0.46 V. A NEGATIVE cell voltage means the reaction cannot happen on its own — it is the exact reverse of the silver tree, which had +0.46 V and works beautifully. This is the real usefulness of the series: it lets you predict that nothing will happen, and put a number to why, without wasting the reagents finding out.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Electrochemistry, predicting feasibility from cell potential

hazard.title: Lead compounds are poisonous
hazard.warning: Both the lead(II) nitrate solution and the lead metal grown from it are poisonous, and lead accumulates in the body rather than being cleared out.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Handle with gloves, wash your hands afterwards, and put all lead waste in the labelled heavy-metal container rather than down the sink.

explanation: The lead tree — the same idea as the silver tree, with feathery grey crystals instead of bright needles. Zinc is at −0.76 V and lead at −0.13 V, giving a cell voltage of −0.13 − (−0.76) = +0.63 V: positive, so it goes, but a smaller voltage than the silver version and correspondingly less dramatic. Three trees grown side by side — silver from zinc, silver from copper, lead from zinc — put the whole electrochemical series in front of you as a set of visible speeds.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Electrochemistry, electrochemical series; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (standard electrode potentials)

explanation: No observable change. Copper is at +0.34 V and lead at −0.13 V, so the cell voltage is −0.13 − 0.34 = −0.47 V, and a negative value means it will not go. Lead sits ABOVE copper in the series, so lead can displace copper but copper cannot displace lead. This pair is worth doing right after the zinc and lead one: same lead solution, different metal, and the series correctly predicts one works and one does not.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Electrochemistry, predicting feasibility from cell potential

explanation: Zinc at −0.76 V displaces iron at −0.44 V, a cell voltage of +0.32 V. That is the smallest positive value in this batch and the reaction is correspondingly slow and undramatic — the pale green of the iron(II) solution fades and a dark deposit collects on the zinc. It matters far beyond the beaker: because zinc is the more reactive of the two, a zinc coating on iron protects it even when scratched, which is what galvanising is and why it works when paint alone does not.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Electrochemistry, electrochemical series and sacrificial protection

explanation: Magnesium sits right down at −2.37 V, so against iron's −0.44 V the cell voltage is +1.93 V — the largest in this batch, and the reaction is correspondingly the most vigorous, with the mixture warming noticeably. Set this against zinc and iron at +0.32 V and the pattern is unmistakable: the bigger the gap in the series, the bigger the voltage and the more energy comes out. Magnesium's position is also why blocks of it are bolted to ships' hulls and buried pipelines, to corrode away in place of the iron.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Electrochemistry, electrochemical series and sacrificial protection

effects.precipitate: bright silver plated on the cathode

cathode.observation: A bright, even layer of silver plates onto whatever object is made the cathode.

anode.observation: Oxygen bubbles off, because the nitrate ion is not discharged.

explanation: Silver plating, and the reason electroplating is done at all: a cheap object made the cathode comes out covered in an even, hard-wearing layer of an expensive metal. Only one electron is needed per silver ion, unlike two for copper, so the deposit builds quickly. At the anode the nitrate ion is too stable to give up electrons, so hydroxide ions from the water do it instead and oxygen comes off — which is why the solution turns increasingly acidic as the plating goes on.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Electrochemistry, electroplating

effects.precipitate: reddish brown copper on the cathode

cathode.observation: Reddish-brown copper coats the electrode and the blue-green colour fades.

anode.observation: Pale green chlorine bubbles off and bleaches damp litmus held near it.

hazard.title: Poisonous chlorine gas is released
hazard.warning: Chlorine given off at the anode is poisonous to breathe and irritates the eyes and lungs.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Electrolyse only small volumes in a fume cupboard or a very well ventilated room, and never lean over the cell.

explanation: The tidiest electrolysis of a solution there is, and the one to learn the rules from: BOTH products come from the dissolved salt itself rather than from the water. Copper is below hydrogen in the series so the copper ion is discharged in preference to the water at the cathode, and the chloride is discharged in preference to the water at the anode. Compare it with brine, where the sodium is too reactive to be discharged and hydrogen appears instead — same setup, different answer, and the electrochemical series is what tells the two apart.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Electrochemistry, electrolysis of solutions and preferential discharge

effects.precipitate: molten aluminium collecting at the base

cathode.observation: Molten aluminium collects on the carbon lining at the base of the cell and is tapped off.

anode.observation: Oxygen burns the carbon anodes away, so they have to be replaced continually.

hazard.title: A cell of molten salt at nearly 1000 °C
hazard.warning: This runs as a bath of molten material at about 950 °C carrying an enormous current, with molten metal collecting underneath. Any water reaching molten metal flashes to steam instantly and throws it out of the cell.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: This is an industrial smelter, shown here as a simulation. It is not something to attempt in a school laboratory — study the cell diagram and the half equations instead.

explanation: How aluminium is actually made. It is far too reactive to be extracted by heating its ore with carbon the way iron is, so the only route is electrolysis — and that is why aluminium was once more precious than gold, and stayed a curiosity until electricity became cheap. Aluminium oxide melts above 2000 °C, which would be impossible to run; dissolving it in molten cryolite brings that down to about 950 °C. Even so the process consumes so much electricity that smelters are built next to power stations, and recycling aluminium takes about a twentieth of the energy of making it new.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XI — Electrochemistry, extraction of aluminium by electrolysis

hazard.title: Flammable hydrogen, and a strongly alkaline solution
hazard.warning: Lithium is the gentlest of the alkali metals with water, but it still gives off hydrogen steadily and leaves a solution alkaline enough to attack skin and eyes.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Use a small piece behind a safety screen, keep flames away, and wear eye protection. Never touch alkali metals with bare or damp hands.

explanation: The first of three to be done side by side, because the comparison is the whole lesson. Lithium floats — it is the least dense solid element known, at about half the density of water — and fizzes steadily without melting. It stays a recognisable piece of metal throughout. Keep this picture in mind for what sodium and potassium do next.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group IA elements, reaction with water

hazard.title: Sodium reacts violently with water
hazard.warning: Sodium melts from its own heat, skates across the surface, and can catch fire or spit molten metal. The sodium hydroxide left behind is strongly caustic. A piece larger than a grain of rice is genuinely dangerous.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: This is a teacher demonstration behind a safety screen, using a piece no bigger than a grain of rice on a large trough of water. Never put alkali metals in a sink, and never use more than the smallest visible piece.

explanation: The middle of the three, and the change from lithium is unmistakable. Enough heat comes out that the sodium MELTS into a silver ball and skates about the surface, fizzing hard. The reason is that sodium's outer electron sits further from the nucleus than lithium's and is more loosely held, so it is given up more easily. That is why reactivity increases going DOWN Group I — the opposite direction to Group VII, and one of the most commonly muddled points in the syllabus.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group IA elements, reaction with water and the trend in reactivity

hazard.title: Potassium reacts explosively with water
hazard.warning: Potassium reacts fast enough that the hydrogen it produces ignites on its own, burning with a lilac flame, and the piece can spit and explode. It is more violent than sodium and gives no time to react once started.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: A teacher demonstration only, behind a safety screen, with the smallest possible piece on a large trough. Never attempt this as a student experiment.

explanation: The third of the three, and it completes the trend beyond doubt. Potassium reacts so fast that the hydrogen catches fire as it is produced, burning with the lilac flame that identifies potassium — so this reaction gives you the flame test for free. Lithium fizzes, sodium melts and darts, potassium ignites: three metals in one group, one clear direction, and the explanation is simply how far the outer electron sits from the nucleus.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group IA elements, reaction with water and the trend in reactivity

explanation: Lithium burns in air with a crimson flame to give the plain oxide, Li₂O — and it is the ONLY alkali metal that does. Everything about Group I encourages the idea that its members behave alike, so it is worth meeting the place where they do not: burn sodium and you get the peroxide instead, burn potassium and you get the superoxide. Lithium is the odd one out because its ion is small enough to hold a simple oxide ion stably.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group IA elements, reactions with oxygen

explanation: Sodium burns in plenty of air with its familiar golden-yellow flame, but what it leaves is NOT the simple oxide — it is the pale yellow peroxide, with an oxygen–oxygen bond still intact. Put this next to lithium and the neat picture of a group behaving as one falls apart in a single experiment. The bigger sodium ion cannot stabilise a lone oxide ion as well, so the peroxide wins. It has a real use: sodium peroxide takes in exhaled carbon dioxide and gives oxygen back, which is why it is carried in submarines and breathing sets.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group IA elements, reactions with oxygen

explanation: Magnesium carbonate breaks down at about 350 °C — hot, but well within a strongly heated test tube, so this is an experiment a class can actually do. Collect the gas and turn limewater milky to prove it is carbon dioxide. Now compare it with calcium carbonate, which needs a kiln at 900 °C, and barium carbonate, which needs over 1300 °C: thermal stability of the carbonates INCREASES down Group II, because the larger cations distort the carbonate ion less and so pull it apart less easily.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group IIA, thermal stability of carbonates

explanation: Limestone into quicklime — one of the oldest industrial processes there is, and still one of the largest. It needs about 900 °C, which is why it is done in a kiln and why a Bunsen burner will not manage it however long you leave it: the app will keep telling you the temperature is not high enough, and that is the honest answer. Set against magnesium carbonate at 350 °C, the pair make the Group II trend concrete. The quicklime produced can then be slaked with water, which is where the lime cycle continues.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group IIA, thermal stability of carbonates; Chemistry XI — Industrial Chemistry, lime

explanation: The Group II hydroxides follow the same rule as the carbonates: magnesium hydroxide gives up its water at about 350 °C, while calcium hydroxide holds on until well over 500 °C and barium hydroxide further still. Stability increases down the group in both families, for the same reason — the larger the cation, the less it distorts and destabilises the anion sitting next to it. The water driven off condenses on the cool part of the tube.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group IIA, thermal stability of hydroxides

explanation: Every Group II carbonate is insoluble, so adding a soluble carbonate to any Group II salt drops the carbonate out as a white solid. This is how the magnesium carbonate for the decomposition experiment is prepared, and it is also the reaction that removes hardness from water — the same chemistry doing a laboratory job here and a domestic one there.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group IIA, solubility of the carbonates

hazard.title: Soluble barium salts are poisonous
hazard.warning: The barium chloride used here is poisonous if swallowed. The barium carbonate formed is far less dangerous because it is almost insoluble, but it does dissolve in stomach acid, so it is not as harmless as barium sulfate.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Handle barium solutions with care, wash your hands afterwards, and put the waste in the labelled heavy-metal container.

explanation: The same reaction one row further down Group II, and worth doing alongside the magnesium one: both give a white precipitate, and the barium one is noticeably denser and settles faster. It is also a useful contrast with barium sulfate — that one is safe enough to swallow for an X-ray because nothing dissolves it, while barium carbonate dissolves in stomach acid and is genuinely poisonous. Insoluble in water does not mean insoluble in everything.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group IIA, solubility of the carbonates

hazard.title: Poisonous chlorine gas is being generated
hazard.warning: This is a chlorine generator. Chlorine attacks the eyes and lungs, is denser than air so it collects low down rather than dispersing, and was used as a chemical weapon. Heating concentrated hydrochloric acid also gives off choking hydrogen chloride fumes.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Run this only in a fume cupboard, generate no more gas than you need, and pass the excess through sodium hydroxide solution to destroy it rather than letting it into the room.

explanation: The standard laboratory preparation of chlorine, and a clean example of redox with both halves visible. Manganese(IV) oxide takes electrons from the chloride ions, so the chloride is oxidised to chlorine gas while the manganese is reduced from +4 down to +2 — which is why the flask ends up holding the very pale pink of a manganese(II) solution. Note that this needs manganese(IV) oxide as a REACTANT, not a catalyst: it is used up here, unlike its role with hydrogen peroxide.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group VIIA, laboratory preparation of chlorine

explanation: How household bleach is made, and a rare thing worth naming: DISPROPORTIONATION. The chlorine starts at oxidation state 0 and ends up in two places at once — reduced to −1 in the chloride, and oxidised to +1 in the hypochlorite. One element, one reaction, oxidised and reduced simultaneously. Doing this cold gives the hypochlorite that bleaches; doing it hot gives the chlorate instead, which is why the temperature is specified on an industrial plant. It is also the safe way to destroy leftover chlorine, which is why a chlorine generator is vented through sodium hydroxide.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group VIIA, reaction of chlorine with cold dilute alkali

hazard.title: Choking hydrogen chloride fumes
hazard.warning: Steamy, acrid fumes of hydrogen chloride come off and fume heavily in moist air. They attack the eyes and airways.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Work in a fume cupboard, and if you are collecting the gas lead it into water rather than letting it escape.

explanation: The first of three, and the control. Concentrated sulfuric acid simply displaces the more volatile hydrogen chloride from its salt — an acid–base swap, with NO redox at all. Nothing is oxidised, nothing is reduced, and the only product besides the salt is steamy hydrogen chloride. Chloride ions are too weakly reducing to attack the sulfuric acid. Keep that in mind for the bromide and iodide, which do exactly that.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group VIIA, reactions of halides with concentrated sulfuric acid

hazard.title: Bromine vapour and sulfur dioxide together
hazard.warning: Orange-brown bromine vapour and choking sulfur dioxide come off at the same time. Bromine burns skin badly on contact and its vapour attacks the eyes and lungs.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard only, on the smallest scale that shows the colour. Never handle bromine or its vapour outside one.

explanation: The second of three, and now something new happens. The bromide starts as the chloride did, but it does not stop there: bromide ions are strong enough reducing agents to attack the sulfuric acid itself, pulling the sulfur from +6 down to +4 as sulfur dioxide, while the bromide is oxidised to orange-brown bromine. Set the three tubes side by side and the trend is unmistakable: reducing power of the halide ions INCREASES down Group VII, because a larger ion holds its outer electrons more loosely and gives them up more readily.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group VIIA, reducing power of the halide ions

hazard.title: Hydrogen sulfide is released
hazard.warning: Hydrogen sulfide smells of rotten eggs and is genuinely poisonous. The danger is that it deadens the sense of smell within minutes, so the warning fades exactly as the concentration rises — people have died believing the gas had cleared.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard only, smallest possible scale. Never rely on the smell to tell you whether it is safe, and leave the room if you notice the smell weakening.

explanation: The third of three, and the trend reaches its conclusion. Iodide ions are the strongest reducing agents of the three, and they do not stop at sulfur dioxide — they drag the sulfur all the way from +6 down to −2, giving hydrogen sulfide, while dark purple iodine appears. Read the set together: chloride does no redox at all, bromide takes the sulfur to +4, iodide takes it to −2. One column of the periodic table, one property, changing steadily as the ion gets larger.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group VIIA, reducing power of the halide ions

effects.dissolves: the white curdy solid went completely, leaving a clear colourless solution

explanation: The white precipitate simply disappears. Two ammonia molecules attach to each silver ion and hold it in solution as a complex ion, so a solid that water could not touch dissolves in front of you. This is the second half of the halide test: silver chloride dissolves in dilute ammonia, silver bromide needs concentrated ammonia, and silver iodide will not dissolve at all. Since white and cream are hard to tell apart by eye, the ammonia test is what actually settles which halide you have.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group VIIA, distinguishing the silver halides with ammonia

explanation: No observable change — the yellow precipitate just sits there. Silver iodide is the least soluble of the three silver halides by a very wide margin, and ammonia cannot pull the silver ion out of it however concentrated it is. That refusal is exactly what makes the test useful: add ammonia to three tubes and the chloride dissolves, the bromide dissolves only if the ammonia is concentrated, and the iodide never does. A negative result identifying a substance is as good as a positive one.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group VIIA, distinguishing the silver halides with ammonia

hazard.title: Hydrogen and chlorine explode together
