hazard.warning: A mixture of hydrogen and chlorine explodes when lit — and, unusually, also when exposed to bright sunlight or a camera flash, with no flame needed at all. The hydrogen chloride produced is corrosive and choking.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: This is an industrial process. Any demonstration is done behind a screen with a tiny volume of gas, and mixtures of the two are never stored or left in daylight.

explanation: The direct synthesis, and how hydrogen chloride is made on an industrial scale for hydrochloric acid. The striking thing is what sets it off: light alone will do it, because a photon splits a chlorine molecule into two very reactive atoms and a chain reaction follows. Combustion usually needs heat; here a bright enough flash is sufficient, which is a memorable way into how reaction mechanisms actually start.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group VIIA, hydrogen halides and their preparation

hazard.title: Mixing bleach with acid releases chlorine
hazard.warning: Bleach and any acid — including limescale remover, toilet cleaner and even vinegar — release chlorine gas on contact. Chlorine attacks the eyes and lungs and is denser than air, so in a small bathroom it collects rather than clearing. This is one of the commonest household poisonings there is, and it happens in seconds.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Never mix bleach with any other cleaning product. If it happens, leave the room at once, open windows from outside the room, and do not go back in to try to clear it up.

explanation: This entry exists to teach what NOT to do. The hypochlorite ion and the chloride ion meet in acid and reverse the disproportionation that made the bleach in the first place, giving chlorine gas straight back. It is the same chemistry as the laboratory preparation, except it happens by accident in a bathroom with no fume cupboard anywhere. Bleach bottles carry the warning for exactly this reason.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group VIIA, reactions of hypochlorites

hazard.title: Toxic gas released
hazard.warning: This combination releases chloramine vapour, which is toxic to inhale. It burns the eyes and airways and can cause lasting lung damage. Because bleach and ammonia-based cleaners are both ordinary household products, this is one of the most frequent accidental poisonings in the home. In a real laboratory this must never be done outside a fume hood.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Never mix chlorine bleach with ammonia-based cleaners, and never combine cleaning products at all in the hope of a stronger result. Ventilate and evacuate if it happens accidentally, and do not re-enter to clean it up.

explanation: The companion warning to bleach with acid, and the other reason two cleaners must never be combined. Ammonia-based glass cleaner poured into a toilet already treated with bleach gives exactly this. The entry is here to teach the danger and the correct response — what to avoid and what to do if it happens — and deliberately not the quantities or method that would help anyone produce it.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group VIIA, reactions of hypochlorites; PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Chloramine

explanation: Variable oxidation state, seen as a colour change. Iron gives up one more electron and goes from +2 to +3, and the pale green of the iron(II) solution turns yellow-brown. This is what marks the transition metals out: a main-group metal like sodium or magnesium has one oxidation state and that is that, while iron has two that are both easy to reach and easy to move between. The half-filled d subshell of Fe³⁺ is part of why the higher state is so accessible here.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Transition Elements, variable oxidation states

explanation: The most sensitive test for iron(III) there is — a trace turns the whole solution blood red, so it will find rust dissolved in water at concentrations nothing else would show. It is also the standard equilibrium demonstration: the double arrow is real, and adding more iron(III) OR more thiocyanate deepens the colour, while removing either fades it. That is Le Chatelier's principle in a form you can photograph, which is why this exact pair appears in every equilibrium chapter.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Transition Elements, complex ions; Chemistry XI — Chemical Equilibrium, Le Chatelier's principle

explanation: The same iron, travelling the other way. Here iron(III) acts as the OXIDISING agent: it takes an electron from each iodide ion and drops back to iron(II), while brown iodine appears. Put this next to the chlorine reaction and the pair make the point — a transition metal ion can be the oxidant in one flask and the thing being oxidised in the next, because both of its states are stable and close in energy. Chlorine is a strong enough oxidant to push iron up; iodide is a strong enough reductant to pull it back down.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Transition Elements, variable oxidation states and redox behaviour

explanation: Add ammonia a little at a time and two things happen in order: first a pale blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide, then — as more ammonia goes in — that precipitate dissolves again into an intense royal blue solution. The ammonia molecules have displaced the water around the copper ion. Same metal, same +2 charge, different ligands, and a completely different colour, which is the clearest evidence that in a complex the colour belongs to the whole ion and not to the metal by itself. It is also a confirmatory test for copper(II).
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Transition Elements, complex formation and ligand exchange

explanation: Warm the pale blue precipitate and it turns black as it loses water and becomes copper(II) oxide. It is a satisfying loop to close: that black oxide is the same substance that dissolves in acid to give a blue-green solution, and the same one hydrogen reduces back to bright copper metal. Three appearances of copper — blue hydroxide, black oxide, red-brown metal — all within a few experiments of each other.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Transition Elements, copper chemistry

hazard.title: Chromium(VI) compounds are toxic and carcinogenic
hazard.warning: Both the orange dichromate and the yellow chromate contain chromium in the +6 state, which is poisonous and causes cancer. They also stain skin and clothing.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Handle with gloves, avoid raising any dust from the solid, and put all chromium waste in the labelled heavy-metal container rather than down the sink.

explanation: Orange to yellow, and the important thing is what has NOT happened: this is not a redox reaction. The chromium is in the +6 state before and after — nothing is oxidised or reduced. All that changes is how the chromium and oxygen are arranged, and the colour changes with it. Add acid and the orange comes straight back, which is why the double arrow is there. It is the cleanest available proof that colour in a transition metal compound depends on the whole ion, not on the oxidation state alone.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Transition Elements, the chromate–dichromate equilibrium

hazard.title: Chromium(VI) compounds are toxic and carcinogenic
hazard.warning: Potassium dichromate contains chromium in the +6 state, which is poisonous and carcinogenic. The mixture is also strongly acidic.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Wear gloves and eye protection, and collect all chromium waste in the labelled heavy-metal container. The green chromium(III) product is much less hazardous than the orange starting material, but it still does not belong down the sink.

explanation: Orange to green, and this time it IS a redox reaction — the contrast with the alkali version is the point of doing both. Dichromate takes three electrons per chromium atom, dropping from +6 to +3, while each iron(II) gives one up and becomes iron(III). Acid is essential: the equation needs fourteen hydrogen ions, which is why nothing happens without it. This colour change is the chemistry the original breathalyser ran on — alcohol in the breath reduced orange dichromate on the tube to green, and how far the green spread gave the reading.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Transition Elements, dichromate as an oxidising agent

explanation: The purple simply vanishes. Manganese falls from +7 all the way to +2 — five oxidation states in a single step — and manganese(II) is so faintly pink that it reads as colourless. That disappearing act makes permanganate SELF-INDICATING: in a titration you add it until one drop leaves a permanent pale pink, and no separate indicator is needed at all. The acid must be sulfuric; hydrochloric would be oxidised to chlorine instead and ruin the result, which is a favourite examination question.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Transition Elements, permanganate as an oxidising agent and redox titrations

explanation: The test for chromium(III): alkali gives a grey-green gelatinous precipitate. What makes it interesting is what happens if you keep adding alkali — the precipitate dissolves again, because chromium(III) hydroxide is AMPHOTERIC and reacts with base as well as acid. Magnesium hydroxide, from a main-group metal, simply sits there however much alkali you add. Adding reagent in excess and watching what happens next is a routine worth having, because the second half of the answer is often where the identification actually lies.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Transition Elements, chromium(III) chemistry and amphoteric hydroxides

effects.precipitate: dark green and black manganese residue

hazard.title: A strong oxidiser being heated
hazard.warning: Potassium permanganate gives up oxygen when hot, and anything combustible in the tube — paper, dust, a trace of glycerol — can ignite fiercely.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Heat only in a clean dry tube, on a small scale, and keep it well away from anything that burns. It stains skin and clothing brown, so wear gloves.

explanation: Another laboratory preparation of oxygen, and a display of manganese's oxidation states in one tube. The purple +7 permanganate breaks into green +6 manganate and black +4 manganese(IV) oxide, releasing oxygen as it goes. Four states of one metal — purple at +7, green at +6, black at +4 and pale pink at +2 — each with its own colour. That is the transition metals in a sentence, and it is why they are the coloured part of the periodic table.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Transition Elements, oxidation states of manganese; preparation of oxygen

hazard.title: Chlorine going in, hydrogen chloride coming out
hazard.warning: Both the chlorine used and the hydrogen chloride produced are choking and attack the lungs. The chloromethane formed is toxic as well.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard only, on the smallest scale. Never mix the two gases and leave them in sunlight — the reaction can start on its own and run away.

explanation: The one thing an alkane will do: SUBSTITUTION, where a hydrogen is swapped out rather than something being added on. There is no double bond for anything to add across, so the molecule has to be attacked instead — either by ultraviolet light at room temperature or by heating to around 400 °C. Both work because both split a chlorine molecule into two free radicals, and those start a chain. The awkwardness is that it does not stop: the chloromethane produced is attacked in its turn, so you always end up with a mixture rather than the one product you wanted.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aliphatic Hydrocarbons, free radical substitution in alkanes

hazard.title: Methane and air are an explosive mixture
hazard.warning: Methane burns readily and forms an explosive mixture with air over a wide range of concentrations. Because it is odourless, a smell is added to domestic gas so that leaks can be noticed at all.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Light the gas at the burner rather than letting it collect first, and never search for a leak with a flame.

explanation: Natural gas burning, and the reaction most of the world's heating and cooking runs on. In PLENTY of air it gives carbon dioxide and water and nothing else. Starve it of air and the same fuel gives carbon monoxide instead — colourless, odourless, and the reason a blocked flue kills people in their sleep. A blue flame means enough air is getting in; a yellow, sooty one means it is not, which is a check worth knowing outside a chemistry lesson.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aliphatic Hydrocarbons, combustion of alkanes

hazard.title: Flammable ethyne is produced, and the mixture gets hot
hazard.warning: Ethyne is highly flammable and the reaction gives out enough heat to be felt. The calcium hydroxide left behind is strongly alkaline.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Add water to the carbide a drop at a time so the gas comes off at a controlled rate, keep flames away until you mean to test the gas, and wear eye protection.

explanation: How ethyne is made in a laboratory: drip water onto calcium carbide and the gas comes off at once. Before electric lighting this was how miners' and cyclists' lamps worked — a carbide chamber, a water drip, and a flame at the top. The gas has a strong garlic-like smell, though that comes from phosphine impurities rather than from ethyne itself, which is odourless when pure.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aliphatic Hydrocarbons, laboratory preparation of ethyne

explanation: THE test for a carbon–carbon double bond, and it could hardly be easier to read: shake the gas with orange bromine water and the orange disappears. The bromine has added ACROSS the double bond, one atom to each carbon, and the product is colourless. Nothing needs heating, no catalyst is required, and it happens on shaking — that readiness is the whole difference between an unsaturated compound and a saturated one.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aliphatic Hydrocarbons, addition reactions of alkenes and the test for unsaturation

explanation: The same test, one step further. A triple bond can add bromine TWICE — first becoming a double bond, then a single one — so ethyne soaks up twice as much bromine water as the same amount of ethene before the orange finally goes. That is how the test distinguishes an alkyne from an alkene instead of merely announcing that something is unsaturated, and measuring the amount absorbed is the principle behind the iodine number used to grade fats and oils.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aliphatic Hydrocarbons, addition reactions of alkynes

explanation: No observable change — the bromine water stays orange. Ethane is SATURATED: every bond is a single bond and there is nothing for the bromine to add across. In the dark and without ultraviolet light it will not substitute either, so absolutely nothing happens. This is the control that gives the other two results their meaning: a test that everything passes tells you nothing, and it is only because ethane fails to decolourise bromine water that ethene decolourising it proves anything at all.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aliphatic Hydrocarbons, distinguishing saturated from unsaturated compounds

explanation: Hydrogen adds across the double bond over a nickel catalyst, turning an alkene into an alkane. This is the reaction that hardens liquid vegetable oils into margarine: their long chains contain double bonds, and hydrogenating some of them raises the melting point until the oil becomes a spreadable solid. Nickel is used rather than platinum for one reason only — it is far cheaper and does the same job. Note the catalyst is still there at the end; only the hydrogen and ethene are consumed.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aliphatic Hydrocarbons, catalytic hydrogenation of alkenes

explanation: Hydrogen adds to a triple bond one stage at a time: ethyne first becomes ethene, and only with more hydrogen does the ethene go on to ethane. Add hydrogen to this vessel again and you can watch the second stage happen. Stopping cleanly at the alkene is genuinely difficult and needs a deliberately weakened catalyst, which is a real industrial problem rather than a textbook detail — it is how partially hydrogenated fats came about.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aliphatic Hydrocarbons, catalytic hydrogenation of alkynes

explanation: Water adds across the double bond over phosphoric acid, and this is how most industrial ethanol is made — not by fermentation. The two routes are worth comparing: this one is fast, continuous and gives a pure product, but starts from crude oil; fermentation is slow and gives a dilute mixture, but starts from sugar and is renewable. Which is better depends on what you are optimising for, and that is a genuine judgement rather than a fact to memorise.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aliphatic Hydrocarbons, industrial hydration of ethene

explanation: Baeyer's test — the second way of showing a double bond is there. Cold dilute permanganate attacks the double bond and puts an OH group on each carbon, giving a diol. Two things happen that you can see at once: the purple is destroyed, and a brown precipitate of manganese(IV) oxide appears. Having a second, independent test matters, because bromine water can be decolourised by other things too, and two tests agreeing is much stronger evidence than one. The product here is the antifreeze in car radiators.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aliphatic Hydrocarbons, Baeyer's test for unsaturation

hazard.title: Benzene causes cancer, and hydrogen bromide is corrosive
hazard.warning: Benzene is a proven carcinogen — it is absorbed through skin as well as breathed, and there is no concentration considered safe for casual handling. The hydrogen bromide given off is choking and corrosive.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: This is why school laboratories use methylbenzene instead of benzene wherever they can. If benzene must be used it is a fume cupboard job with gloves throughout, and never on an open bench.

explanation: The single most important thing about benzene, and it shows up twice here. FIRST: with no catalyst present, nothing happens at all — the app will simply say a catalyst is missing. Shake ethene with bromine water and the orange vanishes on the spot; shake benzene with it and the orange stays. Benzene looks unsaturated on paper and refuses to behave like it, because its six spare electrons are spread evenly round the whole ring and breaking that arrangement costs more than the reaction gains. SECOND: once the catalyst polarises the bromine enough to force a reaction, what happens is SUBSTITUTION, not addition — a hydrogen is swapped out, the ring survives intact, and the hydrogen bromide fuming off is the proof.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aromatic Hydrocarbons, electrophilic substitution and the stability of the ring

hazard.title: Benzene, a nitrating mixture, and nitrobenzene - all three are dangerous
hazard.warning: Benzene causes cancer. The concentrated acid mixture is fiercely corrosive and gets hot on mixing. Nitrobenzene smells pleasantly of almonds and is absorbed straight through skin, where it stops the blood carrying oxygen — the smell is an invitation to a serious poisoning.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard, gloves and eye protection throughout, and the temperature held below 60 °C in a water bath — a runaway here can produce dinitrobenzene explosively. Never judge nitrobenzene safe because it smells sweet.

explanation: Nitration, and the reaction that founded the synthetic dye and explosives industries. Sulfuric acid's job is to take a hydrogen from the nitric acid and generate the nitronium ion, which is what actually attacks the ring — the nitric acid alone is not reactive enough. Note that once again the ring survives: a hydrogen is substituted and the delocalised system is left whole. Nitrobenzene goes on to become aniline and from there most of the early synthetic dyes.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aromatic Hydrocarbons, nitration of benzene

hazard.title: Benzene causes cancer and the acid is fuming
hazard.warning: Benzene is a proven carcinogen absorbed through skin as well as lungs. Fuming sulfuric acid attacks skin and eyes instantly and the mixture must be heated.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard with gloves and a face shield, heated in a water bath rather than over a flame. Add the acid to the benzene slowly and never the reverse.

explanation: The third substitution on the ring, and the one with the biggest industrial output. What it produces is a molecule of two halves: a benzene ring that will not mix with water at one end, and a strongly acidic group that dissolves readily at the other. That is precisely the structure of a detergent — the hydrocarbon tail grips grease, the sulfonate head is dragged away by water, and the two together lift the dirt off. Almost every washing-up liquid and washing powder starts here.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aromatic Hydrocarbons, sulfonation and detergent manufacture

hazard.title: Burning a carcinogen, and the soot is carcinogenic too
hazard.warning: Benzene causes cancer, and the thick black smoke it burns with carries unburnt aromatic compounds that are carcinogenic in their own right. The flame is also very hot and benzene vapour ignites easily.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard only, and burn the smallest quantity that shows the effect. The sooty flame is the point of the demonstration, so a drop on a watch glass is plenty.

explanation: Benzene burns with a strikingly smoky yellow flame, thick with soot, and that appearance is itself a clue to the structure. The proportion of carbon in an aromatic ring is so high that ordinary air cannot supply enough oxygen to burn it all, and the surplus carbon comes off as smoke. Compare it with methane's clean blue flame: the sootier the flame, the more carbon-rich the fuel, which is a quick qualitative test for an aromatic compound.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aromatic Hydrocarbons, combustion of benzene

explanation: Benzene CAN be made to add hydrogen — but look at what it takes. Ethene does this over nickel at ordinary temperatures; benzene needs about 180 °C and high pressure, and it takes three molecules of hydrogen all at once rather than one. There is no stopping half way at a partly hydrogenated ring, because breaking the delocalisation is the expensive step and once it is paid for the rest follows. That contrast in conditions is the best measure there is of how much the delocalised ring is worth, and the product is a puckered chair-shaped ring rather than a flat one.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aromatic Hydrocarbons, hydrogenation and resonance energy

explanation: Nucleophilic substitution, and half of the most instructive pair in the whole of organic chemistry. The carbon–bromine bond is polar, leaving that carbon slightly positive; the hydroxide ion has a lone pair and is drawn straight to it, pushing the bromide out as it arrives. In WATER this is what happens and you get an alcohol. Now do the identical reaction in ethanol instead and see what changes.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Alkyl Halides, nucleophilic substitution

explanation: The other half of the pair, and the reason conditions get written under arrows. Same halogenoalkane, same sodium hydroxide, same heat — but dissolved in ethanol rather than water, the hydroxide stops behaving as a nucleophile and behaves as a BASE instead. Rather than attacking the carbon, it pulls a hydrogen off the neighbouring one, and the electrons left behind form a double bond as the bromide departs. Substitution gives an alcohol; elimination gives an alkene. Nothing about the reagents predicts which — only the solvent does, and you can confirm the difference by testing the gas with bromine water.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Alkyl Halides, elimination versus substitution

explanation: Ammonia has a lone pair on its nitrogen, so it too is a nucleophile and attacks the same slightly positive carbon, giving an amine. The awkwardness is that the amine produced ALSO has a lone pair on its nitrogen and is if anything a better nucleophile than ammonia was — so it attacks more bromoethane in its turn, and the real product is a mixture of primary, secondary and tertiary amines. Using a large excess of ammonia improves the odds without ever fixing the problem, which is a good early lesson in why a clean equation on paper does not guarantee a clean product in a flask.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Alkyl Halides, reaction with ammonia

equation: C₂H₅Br + AgNO₃ + H₂O → AgBr + C₂H₅OH + HNO₃
explanation: The test that identifies which halogen a halogenoalkane contains. Warming it with silver nitrate lets the halide leave and it drops out as the silver halide, with the same colours as always — white for chloride, cream for bromide, yellow for iodide. What makes it more than a repeat of the halide test is the SPEED: the iodide goes first, the bromide next and the chloride slowest, because the carbon–halogen bond gets weaker down the group and so breaks more easily. Timing three tubes side by side turns bond strength into something you can watch.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Alkyl Halides, identifying the halogen and carbon–halogen bond strength

hazard.title: Hot concentrated sulfuric acid
hazard.warning: This needs concentrated sulfuric acid at about 170 °C. At that temperature it chars anything organic it touches, including skin, and the mixture can froth up suddenly.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Heat gently with anti-bumping granules in the flask, wear eye protection and gloves, and never seal the apparatus — the gas must be free to escape.

explanation: Ethanol loses water and becomes ethene, which closes a loop: hydrate ethene and you get ethanol, dehydrate ethanol and you get ethene back. Which direction runs depends entirely on the conditions — phosphoric acid with steam going one way, hot concentrated sulfuric acid going the other. The temperature matters more than it looks: at about 170 °C you get ethene, but nearer 140 °C the same flask gives ethoxyethane instead. This is also the laboratory way to make ethene from something renewable, since the ethanol can come from fermentation.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Alcohols, dehydration to alkenes

hazard.title: Sodium and a flammable solvent
hazard.warning: Hydrogen is given off next to a liquid that itself catches fire easily, and the sodium is corrosive to skin. This is far gentler than sodium in water, but it is still sodium.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Use a small piece of sodium in plenty of ethanol, keep flames away, and destroy any leftover sodium properly rather than putting it in a bin or a sink.

explanation: Sodium fizzes steadily in ethanol and gives off hydrogen — noticeably calmer than the same sodium in water, which is the first hint that the OH here holds its hydrogen more tightly than water does. That makes ethanol an acid, but an extremely weak one. The proof is what is left behind: sodium ethoxide is a stronger base than sodium hydroxide, and the weaker the acid, the stronger the base it leaves. Compare this with the next entry, where sodium hydroxide cannot touch ethanol at all.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Alcohols, reaction with sodium

explanation: No observable change, and that absence is the whole point. Ethanol has an OH group and sodium hydroxide is a strong base, so it looks as though something ought to happen — and nothing does. Ethanol is simply too weak an acid for hydroxide to take its hydrogen. Put this beside the sodium reaction, which DOES work, and beside phenol, which reacts with sodium hydroxide readily, and an order appears: ethanol is a weaker acid than phenol, which is weaker than ethanoic acid. Three tubes, three results, one ladder.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Alcohols and Phenols, comparative acidity

hazard.title: Phenol burns skin, and the burn does not hurt at first
hazard.warning: Phenol causes severe burns, and it numbs the nerves as it does so — so a serious burn can feel mild until the damage is done. It is also absorbed through the skin and is toxic that way.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Gloves and eye protection throughout, and never handle the solid with bare hands. Wash any contact with plenty of water immediately, whether or not it hurts.

explanation: Phenol does what ethanol could not: it hands its hydrogen to sodium hydroxide and dissolves as the salt. The difference is the benzene ring. In ethanol the negative charge left on the oxygen has nowhere to go and sits there, which makes losing the hydrogen expensive; in phenol that charge is spread out round the whole ring, which makes it much cheaper. Same OH group, different neighbour, and an acidity difference of about five orders of magnitude.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Phenols, acidity and delocalisation

hazard.title: Chromium(VI) is carcinogenic and ethanal is volatile and toxic
hazard.warning: Potassium dichromate is poisonous and causes cancer. Ethanal boils at 21 °C, so it comes off as a vapour that is itself toxic and highly flammable.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Gloves and eye protection, collect the distillate rather than letting the vapour into the room, and put all chromium waste in the labelled heavy-metal container.

explanation: The first rung of the oxidation ladder, and orange turns green as the dichromate is reduced. The practical difficulty is that the reaction does not want to stop here: ethanal is easier to oxidise than the ethanol was, so leaving it in the flask means it goes straight on to the acid. The answer is to exploit its low boiling point of 21 °C and DISTIL IT OFF as it forms. Same reagents, same flask — whether you get the aldehyde or the acid depends on the apparatus, which is why the diagram matters as much as the equation.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Alcohols, oxidation of primary alcohols

explanation: The second rung: the aldehyde becomes the carboxylic acid. It goes so readily because the carbonyl carbon still carries a hydrogen, and taking that off is all the oxidation requires. This is why aldehydes are reducing agents in their own right and why every test that identifies them works by letting them reduce something else. A ketone has no such hydrogen and stops dead here — which is the whole basis of the two tests that follow. To make the acid deliberately you use excess dichromate and REFLUX, so nothing escapes until the oxidation is complete.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aldehydes and Ketones, oxidation to carboxylic acids

effects.precipitate: a mirror of silver on the glass

explanation: The silver mirror test, and one of the most striking things a school laboratory does: warm the tube gently and a bright mirror of silver plates itself onto the inside of the glass. The aldehyde is oxidised to the acid, and in giving those electrons up it reduces silver ions to silver metal. Only an aldehyde does this. The same reaction was once the industrial way of silvering mirrors, and it is why glucose — which has an aldehyde group — gives a positive result and is called a reducing sugar.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aldehydes and Ketones, Tollens' test

explanation: No observable change — no mirror, no darkening, nothing. Propanone is a KETONE: its carbonyl carbon sits between two carbon groups and carries no hydrogen of its own, so there is nothing to remove without breaking the carbon chain, and it cannot reduce the silver. That negative result is exactly as informative as the positive one from ethanal. Run the two tubes side by side and you have distinguished an aldehyde from a ketone — two compounds that both contain a C=O group and can look identical on paper.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aldehydes and Ketones, distinguishing aldehydes from ketones

explanation: The second aldehyde test, and it works the same way with a different metal: the aldehyde reduces copper(II) to copper(I), and the deep blue solution throws down a brick-red precipitate. Having two independent tests matters, because a single positive result can always be a coincidence and two agreeing is much harder to argue with. Propanone gives nothing here either, for the same reason it gives nothing with Tollens'. This test was used for a century to check urine for sugar, since glucose reduces the copper in exactly this way.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aldehydes and Ketones, Fehling's test

explanation: Ethanoic acid fizzes with a carbonate exactly as hydrochloric acid does, which settles the question of whether a carboxylic acid is a real acid: it is, weak or not. This is also the test that completes the acidity ladder. Phenol, put with sodium carbonate, does nothing — it is acidic enough for sodium hydroxide but not enough to drive carbon dioxide out of a carbonate. So: ethanol reacts with neither, phenol reacts with hydroxide only, and the carboxylic acid reacts with both. Three compounds, all with an O–H, in a clear order.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Carboxylic Acids, reaction with carbonates and comparative acidity

explanation: Warm an acid with an alcohol and a trace of sulfuric acid and the flask fills with the smell of pear drops. It is the most memorable reaction in the syllabus for a reason — two starting materials that smell of nothing pleasant give something that smells of sweets. Note the double arrow: this is a genuine equilibrium and never goes to completion, so the yield is improved by removing the ester as it forms or by using an excess of one reactant. The sulfuric acid is a catalyst and is not used up, and esters like this one give fruit and flowers much of their scent.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Carboxylic Acids, esterification

hazard.title: Choking fumes of hydrogen chloride
hazard.warning: Steamy hydrogen chloride pours off immediately and attacks the eyes, nose and lungs. Phosphorus pentachloride itself burns skin, and it reacts violently with any water it meets — including the moisture in your breath and on your hands.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard, gloves and eye protection, and keep the reagent bottle stoppered so it stays dry. Never add water to try to quieten it down — that makes the fumes worse, not better.

explanation: Steamy fumes the instant the two meet, and that is the point: this is the standard laboratory TEST for an —OH group. Alcohols, phenols and carboxylic acids all give the fumes; esters, aldehydes and ketones give none, because they have no —OH to attack. What the reaction is doing is swapping that —OH for a chlorine, which turns a sluggish acid into the most reactive derivative there is. One honest note about this simulation: in the real laboratory the acid must be GLACIAL — water-free — because phosphorus pentachloride attacks water just as eagerly as it attacks the acid, and a wet sample simply wastes the reagent.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Carboxylic Acids, reaction with phosphorus pentachloride

hazard.title: Hisses violently and throws off corrosive fumes
hazard.warning: The reaction is immediate and strongly exothermic. It spits, it steams, and the hydrogen chloride coming off burns the airways. Adding water to a bottle of ethanoyl chloride can eject the contents.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard, face protection, and add the ethanoyl chloride dropwise to a large volume of cold water — never the other way round. Destroy small residues this way deliberately rather than leaving them to meet water by accident.

explanation: It hisses on contact with cold water — no heating, no catalyst, no waiting. Compare that with the ester made in the last batch, which needs boiling with alkali before it will break apart at all, and with an amide, which needs prolonged boiling. Same underlying reaction, wildly different speeds, and the reason is the chlorine: it drags electrons away from the carbonyl carbon and leaves it exposed. This is why an acid chloride cannot be stored in a damp bottle, and why it fumes when you simply take the stopper out — it is reacting with the water vapour in the room.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Carboxylic acid derivatives, hydrolysis of acid chlorides

hazard.title: Vigorous, and the fumes are corrosive
hazard.warning: The reaction is fast and gives out heat, and the hydrogen chloride it produces is choking and corrosive. Ethanol is also flammable, and the mixture warms itself considerably.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard, add the acid chloride slowly with cooling, and keep it well away from flames.

explanation: Put this side by side with the esterification from the last batch and the lesson is unmistakable. That one needed an acid catalyst, needed heating, and still stopped at an equilibrium that never went to completion. This one needs neither catalyst nor heat, is over in seconds, and goes the whole way — because the hydrogen chloride escapes as a gas and can never come back to reverse it. The same ester, by two routes: one slow and reversible, one fast and complete. When yield matters, this is the route chemists take.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Carboxylic acid derivatives, reaction of acid chlorides with alcohols

hazard.title: Violent, with dense white smoke
hazard.warning: The two react at once and strongly, and the flask fills with dense white smoke. Ammonia vapour is choking in its own right, and the mixture gets hot enough to spit.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard, eye protection, and add the acid chloride a drop at a time to excess cold ammonia solution.

explanation: A dense white smoke fills the flask and a white solid appears. The chlorine has been replaced by —NH₂ and the product is an AMIDE. Two molecules of ammonia are needed rather than one, because the second is used up mopping the hydrogen chloride into ammonium chloride. Look carefully at the C—N bond that has just been made: repeat it along a chain and it becomes the peptide link that holds every protein in your body together. The bottom rung of this ladder is where biology begins.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Carboxylic acid derivatives, reaction of acid chlorides with ammonia

hazard.title: Both the reagent and the product burn skin and eyes
hazard.warning: Ethanoyl chloride and ethanoic anhydride are corrosive, and the anhydride's vapour makes the eyes stream.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard, gloves and eye protection. Keep everything dry, since both compounds are attacked by water.

explanation: Two ethanoic acid units joined through a shared oxygen — an ANHYDRIDE, which is the second rung of the ladder. It does everything the acid chloride does, with water, with alcohols and with ammonia, but more slowly and without throwing off corrosive hydrogen chloride. That is exactly why industry prefers it: it is easier to control, cheaper, and it is the reagent used to make aspirin. So the full order of reactivity runs acid chloride, then anhydride, then ester, then amide — and each step down that list means a reaction that needs more persuading.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Carboxylic acid derivatives, preparation of anhydrides

explanation: Boil the ester with sodium hydroxide and the fruity smell disappears — the surest sign that the ester has gone. This is the reverse of making it, but done in a way that cannot reverse itself: the acid produced is immediately taken by the alkali as its salt, and a salt will not re-esterify. That is the trick. Acid hydrolysis of the same ester gets stuck at an equilibrium, exactly as making it did, while alkaline hydrolysis goes to completion every time. Note also that heat is genuinely needed here, where the acid chloride hissed in cold water — the ladder again.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Carboxylic acid derivatives, alkaline hydrolysis of esters

hazard.title: Ammonia gas is choking
hazard.warning: Ammonia comes off as the mixture boils and is sharply irritating to the eyes and lungs. Hot sodium hydroxide also burns skin badly and is particularly dangerous to eyes.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard or good ventilation, eye protection, and smell the gas only by wafting it towards you — never by putting your face over the tube.

explanation: Boil an amide with alkali and ammonia is driven off — the test is to hold damp red litmus at the mouth of the tube and watch it turn blue. This is also the last rung of the ladder, and note how much persuading it takes: the acid chloride reacted with cold water on contact, the ester needed boiling with alkali, and the amide needs PROLONGED boiling with it. Two things follow. Ethanamide is neutral rather than basic, because the carbonyl group holds the nitrogen's lone pair away from any passing acid. And since a protein is a chain of amide links, this stubbornness is precisely why your body needs enzymes to digest one.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Carboxylic acid derivatives, hydrolysis of amides

hazard.title: Boiling caustic alkali
hazard.warning: Hot concentrated sodium hydroxide is severely corrosive and the mixture can bump and splash as it boils. Alkali in the eye causes permanent damage within seconds.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Goggles, not just safety spectacles. Heat gently with stirring, use anti-bumping granules, and never lean over the beaker.

explanation: SAPONIFICATION — soap making, and the oldest deliberate chemical reaction there is. Nothing new is happening: a fat IS an ester, three fatty-acid chains joined to one glycerol, and boiling it with alkali hydrolyses it exactly as the last reaction hydrolysed ethyl ethanoate. Three chains come off as the sodium salts, which are the soap, and the glycerol that held them is left behind as a valuable by-product for creams and medicines. Add common salt at the end and the soap, which will not dissolve in brine, rises to the top to be skimmed off.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, saponification and soap manufacture

effects.precipitate: a grey curdy scum instead of a lather

explanation: Shake soap with hard water and you get no lather — just a grey curdy scum and a ring round the bath. Calcium carries two positive charges where sodium carried one, so it grips two soap molecules at once and the result will not dissolve. The soap that becomes scum has done no washing at all, and it goes on being wasted until every calcium ion in the water has been used up. Note which hard water this is: permanent hardness, from calcium sulfate, which BOILING WILL NOT REMOVE. Boiling deals only with the temporary kind.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, action of hard water on soap; Chemistry X — Water, hardness

explanation: No scum, no curd, and a good lather — which is the entire reason synthetic detergents were invented. A detergent is built to the same two-ended plan as soap, but its water-loving head is a sulfonate rather than a —COO⁻, and the calcium salt of a sulfonate stays dissolved instead of precipitating out. Run this beside the soap tube and one shake tells the whole story. Detergents are also close to neutral, where soap is alkaline, so they are safe on wool and silk. The cost came later: the early branched-chain detergents would not break down in rivers and foamed up sewage works, which is why straight-chain ones replaced them.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, soaps and detergents compared

explanation: Exactly the same brick-red result that ethanal gave, and for exactly the same reason: glucose has an aldehyde group, so it is a REDUCING SUGAR. Nothing new is being learnt here — a test met in a bottle of laboratory chemicals is being turned on something out of the kitchen, and it works. One subtlety worth knowing: almost all the glucose in the solution is curled into a ring at any moment, with only a trace in the open-chain aldehyde form. That trace is still enough, because as fast as it is used up more ring opens to replace it, until the whole sample has reacted.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, reducing sugars and Fehling's test

explanation: The solution stays blue — no red precipitate, however long you warm it. Starch is hundreds of glucose units joined end to end, and every link uses up the very carbon that would otherwise open into an aldehyde. Only the one unit at the far end of the chain still has a free reducing group, and one in several hundred is far too dilute to see. So a food packed with glucose can still fail the test for glucose, simply because of how that glucose is joined together. The next two entries show how to unlock it.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, polysaccharides are non-reducing

explanation: One drop of iodine into starch and the whole beaker goes blue-black instantly — the sharpest colour change in school chemistry, and sensitive enough to detect starch at a few parts per million. Be careful how you describe what has happened, because no bond has been made. The starch chain coils into a helix, and iodine molecules slide into the tube down the middle of it; the colour comes from being trapped, not from reacting. In a real laboratory you can prove that for yourself: warm the tube and the colour disappears as the helix unwinds, cool it and the colour comes straight back. A genuine reaction would not do that.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, iodine test for starch

explanation: Boil starch with dilute acid and the chain is cut back to the glucose it was built from — the milky cloudiness clears as it goes. Every link in that chain is an ester-like bond between two sugars, so this is hydrolysis, the same idea that broke the ester and the amide open in the last batch. Your own body does it far more gently, with an enzyme in saliva rather than boiling acid, which is why bread starts to taste sweet if you chew it long enough. IMPORTANT in the real laboratory: neutralise the acid before adding Fehling's, or the alkali in the reagent is simply used up by the acid and the test tells you nothing.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, acid hydrolysis of starch

explanation: The iodine keeps its own brown colour and nothing turns blue — which is precisely the result you want. There is no helix left to trap the iodine, because the starch has been cut into single glucose units. Run this straight after the hydrolysis and it is your proof that the job is finished: the iodine test has gone negative while the Fehling's test has gone positive, and the two together say more than either alone. This is how a chemist checks a reaction is complete rather than guessing.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, testing for completeness of hydrolysis

explanation: Table sugar fails the test for sugar, and the reason is a genuinely good piece of chemistry. Sucrose is one glucose joined to one fructose, and the join is made through exactly the carbon on each half that would otherwise open into a reducing group. Both are tied up at once, so nothing is left to reduce the copper. This is what NON-reducing means. Compare it with glucose, which passes, and it is clear the test is detecting a free reducing group rather than sweetness or the word sugar.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, reducing and non-reducing sugars

explanation: Warm sucrose with dilute acid and the single link holding its two halves together is cut, giving an equal mixture of glucose and fructose. That mixture has a name of its own — INVERT SUGAR — and it is most of what honey is, which is why honey tastes sweeter than table sugar. Nothing has been added or taken away except a molecule of water. As with starch, neutralise the acid before testing with Fehling's.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, hydrolysis of sucrose

explanation: The payoff. Sucrose gave nothing at all with Fehling's; hydrolyse it and the very same test now goes brick red. Nothing was added that could reduce copper — one bond was broken, and that was enough to free the reducing groups on both halves. This pairing is the whole method of carbohydrate chemistry in two tubes: test, then break, then test again, and the difference tells you what was there. Fructose is worth a second look here, because it is a ketone and by the rule from the last batch ought to fail — it passes because the alkali in Fehling's rearranges it into glucose first.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, hydrolysis of sucrose and the reducing test

hazard.title: The reagent is strongly alkaline
hazard.warning: Biuret reagent is copper(II) sulfate in concentrated sodium hydroxide. It burns skin and is particularly dangerous to eyes, where alkali causes lasting damage within seconds.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Goggles and gloves, and rinse any splash with plenty of water at once.

explanation: Pale blue turns violet, and a protein has been identified. What the test actually detects is the PEPTIDE LINK — the same C—N bond made in the last batch when the acid chloride met ammonia — because copper(II) is gripped by the nitrogens of several links at once and that grip changes its colour. Two consequences follow. A single amino acid gives nothing, since there is no link to grip; you need at least three joined together. And the deeper the violet, the more protein there is, which is how protein is measured rather than merely detected.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, biuret test for proteins

effects.precipitate: a solid white coagulate, like cooked egg white

explanation: Warm it past about 60 °C and the clear solution sets to an opaque white solid — an egg cooking, watched as chemistry. Notice what has NOT happened: not one peptide link has broken. The chain is entirely intact; only the folding that held it in shape has been shaken apart, and the unfolded chains have tangled together and dropped out of solution. That is DENATURATION, and it explains why cooling will not undo it — the tangle simply cannot sort itself out again. In a real laboratory a biuret test on the cooked solid still comes out positive, which is the proof that the links survived. The same unfolding is what alcohol does to bacterial proteins, and it is why a disinfectant works.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, denaturation of proteins

equation: NaCl + NH₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → NaHCO₃ + NH₄Cl

effects.precipitate: a fine white solid of sodium hydrogencarbonate

explanation: The heart of the SOLVAY PROCESS, which turns two of the cheapest substances on earth — salt and limestone — into washing soda. Look at what is in the beaker: sodium, ammonium, chloride and hydrogencarbonate ions, which could pair up four different ways. Only one of those four is barely soluble, and that is the one that drops out as a solid. Nothing forces this reaction; it happens because a single product refuses to stay dissolved, and the whole industry rests on that one fact. Bubbling the gas into cold ammoniated brine, not warm, is what keeps it that way.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Common chemical industries, the Solvay process

hazard.title: Ammonia gas is choking
hazard.warning: Ammonia comes off steadily on warming and is sharply irritating to the eyes and lungs. Hot limewater is also caustic.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard or good ventilation, eye protection, and identify the gas by wafting it towards you onto damp red litmus rather than by leaning over the tube.

explanation: This one entry does two jobs. As a laboratory test it is how you prove a salt contains AMMONIUM: warm it with any alkali and ammonia comes off, turning damp red litmus blue — the only common gas that does. As industry it is the step that makes the Solvay process pay. The ammonium chloride left over from the last reaction is treated with cheap lime, and the ammonia comes straight back to be used again. Almost none is consumed overall. A process that had to buy fresh ammonia every cycle would never have been worth building.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Common chemical industries, the Solvay process; Chemistry X — test for the ammonium ion

explanation: Pakistan's largest chemical industry in one line. The ammonia comes from the Haber process and the carbon dioxide is a waste gas from making it, so a plant that would otherwise vent carbon dioxide sells it as fertiliser instead. The real conditions are far beyond a school bench — about 180 °C at 150 atmospheres — and the app simply asks for heat rather than pretending otherwise. This reaction also carries a piece of history: making urea, a compound until then known only from living things, out of two lifeless minerals was what ended the belief that organic matter needed a vital force to create it.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Common chemical industries, manufacture of urea

explanation: An ordinary neutralisation that happens to feed a large part of the world. Watch the pH, though, because it does not land on 7: this is the salt of a WEAK base and a STRONG acid, so the solution comes out ACIDIC. That is not a laboratory curiosity. Fields given this fertiliser season after season slowly sour, and the yield falls until the farmer limes the soil to bring it back. It is still worth using where the crop also needs sulfur, which urea cannot supply — every fertiliser is a trade-off rather than a winner.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Common chemical industries, nitrogenous fertilisers

hazard.title: Ammonium nitrate is a powerful oxidiser
hazard.warning: As a solution in a beaker this is harmless enough. As a bulk solid it is a different matter: ammonium nitrate carries its own oxygen supply, and stored in quantity beside fuel or organic matter, or in a fire, it has caused several of the largest accidental explosions in history.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Never store it near fuels, oils, sawdust or acids, never confine it, and treat any fire near a store of it as an evacuation rather than something to fight. Its sale and storage are regulated in most countries for exactly this reason.

explanation: The other great nitrogen fertiliser, and it beats ammonium sulfate on nitrogen content because BOTH ends of the salt carry nitrogen — the ammonium is taken up slowly and the nitrate immediately. That same double dose of nitrogen is what makes it dangerous in bulk, since the nitrate half is an oxidising agent sitting next to the reducing ammonium half with no need for any air. Useful chemistry and hazardous chemistry are often the same chemistry seen from two sides; here the fertiliser and the explosion have identical formulas.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Common chemical industries, nitrogenous fertilisers

effects.precipitate: hard dark grey nodules of clinker

hazard.title: Cement is alkaline enough to burn skin
hazard.warning: Clinker and the cement ground from it are strongly alkaline once wet — about pH 12.5. Cement burns are common on building sites and are treacherous, because the alkali works slowly and the damage is often done before anything is felt.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Gloves and eye protection, wash any contact off at once with plenty of water however mild it feels, and keep the dust out of the lungs.

explanation: Limestone and clay burnt together in a rotary kiln at about 1450 °C — far past anything a school burner reaches, so the app asks only for heat and leaves the real figure here. The environmental cost is the part worth arguing about: cement accounts for roughly eight per cent of the world's carbon dioxide, and only about half of that comes from the fuel. The rest comes out of the limestone itself, as this equation shows. That half cannot be removed by switching to cleaner fuel — it is built into the chemistry, and it is why cement is such a hard industry to decarbonise.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Common chemical industries, manufacture of cement

equation: Ca₃SiO₅ + H₂O → hydrated calcium silicate + Ca(OH)₂

effects.precipitate: a grey solid mass that hardens as it stands

explanation: Cement does NOT harden by drying, and almost everyone believes it does. It hardens by reacting with the water, growing a mat of interlocking crystals through the space the water occupied — which is why concrete sets perfectly well underwater, why it is kept damp for days after pouring, and why concrete allowed to dry too quickly ends up weaker rather than stronger. The temperature rise here is real and not trivial: a large concrete pour gets hot enough from its own reaction that engineers run cooling pipes through it, and dams have been built in layers for this reason alone.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Common chemical industries, setting and hardening of cement

explanation: The app already knew how to MAKE acid rain — sulfur dioxide from burning coal and diesel, dissolved and oxidised. This is what happens when it lands. Marble and limestone are calcium carbonate, so a building is chemically the same thing as the marble chip in this beaker, and it fizzes away in exactly the same manner. The damage is worse than simple dissolving, because the calcium sulfate left behind takes up more room than the stone it replaced and flakes the surface off, taking carved detail with it. It is why old monuments have blurred faces, and it is a chemistry problem with a political solution: scrub the sulfur out at the chimney.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Environmental chemistry, effects of acid rain

explanation: The remedy, and an honest look at what a remedy is worth. Lakes across Scandinavia and Canada were limed from boats and helicopters through the 1980s to bring acidified water back towards pH 7 so that fish could live in it, and this is the reaction that did it. It works, and it treats the symptom: the moment the liming stops the acid rain is still falling, and the lake goes back. The cure was eventually the unglamorous one — sulfur scrubbers on power stations and low-sulfur fuel — which fixed the cause instead. Notice too that the product is calcium sulfate, so a limed lake ends up harder than it began.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Environmental chemistry, control of acid rain

effects.precipitate: a soft white jelly-like floc that settles slowly

explanation: How muddy river water is made fit to drink, at every waterworks in the country and in any village where a lump of phitkari is rubbed round a pot. The clay that makes water look brown is far too fine to filter and will not settle in a week — the particles all carry the same charge and shove each other apart. Alum cures that in two ways at once: its Al³⁺ ions cancel the charge so the particles can finally touch, and the soft floc forming through the whole depth of the water sweeps them down as it sinks. What is filtered off is mostly the dirt, not the aluminium. It removes bacteria too, but not reliably, which is why chlorination still comes afterwards.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Environmental chemistry, purification of drinking water

effects.precipitate: a grey curdy scum instead of a lather

explanation: Scum again, and the point is that soap cannot tell the two kinds of hardness apart. It is the CALCIUM that wrecks the lather, and calcium is calcium whether it arrived as the hydrogencarbonate or the sulfate. Where the two kinds differ is in how you get rid of them, not in what they do to your soap: this one is temporary hardness, so simply boiling the water first — or adding limewater by Clark's method — removes the calcium and the soap then lathers perfectly. Try that with the sulfate and nothing happens at all. Same symptom, different cure.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry X — Water, temporary hardness and its removal; Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, action of hard water on soap

explanation: A good lather and no scum, exactly as with the other kind of hard water. A detergent does not care which calcium salt it meets, because its sulfonate head makes a calcium salt that stays dissolved either way. That is worth pausing on: boiling fixes temporary hardness and does nothing for permanent, Clark's method fixes temporary and does nothing for permanent, but switching from soap to detergent handles both at once without treating the water at all. Sometimes the cheapest answer to a problem is to stop caring about it.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, soaps and detergents compared

hazard.title: Ammonia gas is choking
hazard.warning: Ammonia comes off steadily on warming and is sharply irritating to the eyes and lungs. Hot limewater is also caustic.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard or good ventilation, eye protection, and identify the gas by wafting it towards you onto damp red litmus rather than by leaning over the tube.

explanation: The ammonium test done with limewater rather than sodium hydroxide, and the result is identical — ANY alkali will do it, because all the test needs is something able to take the hydrogen ion back off the ammonium. That is worth knowing rather than memorising one recipe. Industrially this same reaction is the recovery step of the Solvay process, where cheap lime is used precisely because it is cheap, and the ammonia it releases goes straight back into the plant to be used again.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry X — test for the ammonium ion; Chemistry XII — Common chemical industries, the Solvay process

explanation: Blue to yellow-green, and not one electron has moved. The copper is +2 before and +2 after; all that has changed is what is bonded to it. Four chlorides have pushed six waters off, and because chloride is the bigger ligand only four will fit — so the SHAPE changes too, from octahedral to tetrahedral. That is why the colour changes so completely: the colour of a transition metal complex comes from the gap between its d orbitals, and that gap is set by the ligands and the geometry, not by the metal alone. In the real laboratory this needs concentrated hydrochloric acid, and the intermediate green shows both complexes present at once.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — ligand substitution and the spectrochemical series

explanation: Pink to deep blue. This is the same ligand exchange the copper just did, but with a colour change so complete that it became the standard demonstration of LE CHATELIER'S PRINCIPLE. Adding chloride pushes the equilibrium to the right, and the blue tetrahedral complex takes over. The point of the demonstration is what comes next: nothing has been used up and nothing is irreversible, so adding water pushes it straight back. Try that in the next entry.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — the cobalt(II) chloride equilibrium

explanation: And back to pink, by doing nothing but adding water. This is the half of the demonstration that carries the lesson. An equilibrium is not a reaction that has stopped — it is one running both ways at the same rate, and adding more of something on one side simply shifts where that balance sits. Notice also what water is doing here. It is not a solvent standing politely aside; it is a LIGAND, competing with chloride for the cobalt, and it wins when there is enough of it. Warm the pink solution and it goes blue again, because the change to the blue form absorbs heat.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — the cobalt(II) chloride equilibrium and Le Chatelier's principle

explanation: A rose-red solid appears at once, and almost nothing else on the periodic table does this. Dimethylglyoxime is a CHELATING ligand — one molecule that grips the metal at two points instead of one, like a claw — and the two-point grip is far harder to break than two separate ligands would be. What makes it a great test is the fit. The bite of those two nitrogens matches nickel's square arrangement almost exactly and matches very little else, so the reagent is selective in a way most are not. The precipitate is clean and its composition exact, which is why nickel is one of the few metals still determined by simply filtering, drying and weighing.
source: Vogel's Textbook of Quantitative Chemical Analysis 6th ed. — gravimetric determination of nickel with dimethylglyoxime

effects.dissolves: the white gelatinous solid went completely, leaving a clear solution

explanation: The white solid dissolves and the beaker goes clear — which should be surprising, because a hydroxide is a base and bases do not dissolve in alkali. Aluminium hydroxide does both: it dissolves in acid like any base, and it dissolves in alkali as though it were an acid. That is what AMPHOTERIC means. Industry lives on this one property. Bauxite is aluminium oxide contaminated with iron oxide, and hot alkali dissolves the aluminium and leaves the iron behind — the Bayer process, and the reason aluminium is cheap enough to make drink cans from.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — amphoteric behaviour and the Bayer process

explanation: Nothing dissolves. The solid sits there exactly as it was, and that refusal is one of the most useful facts in qualitative analysis. Ammonia is an alkali, so if aluminium hydroxide dissolved in sodium hydroxide you might expect it to dissolve here too — but ammonia works as a LIGAND rather than simply as a source of hydroxide, and aluminium forms no ammine complexes at all. Zinc hydroxide, which looks identical in the test tube and is also amphoteric, dissolves in ammonia readily. One reagent, two answers, and the two white solids are told apart.
source: Vogel's Textbook of Qualitative Inorganic Analysis 5th ed. — separation of aluminium from zinc

effects.dissolves: the white solid went completely, leaving a clear solution — exactly as the aluminium one did

explanation: Zinc hydroxide dissolves in excess alkali exactly as aluminium's did, giving a colourless solution that looks the same in every respect. So this test has proved that zinc hydroxide is amphoteric, and it has told you nothing whatever about which of the two white solids you are holding. That is worth sitting with. A test that gives the same answer for two possibilities is not a failed test — it has genuinely narrowed things down — but you need a second, different test to finish the job.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — zincate formation

effects.dissolves: the white solid went completely, where aluminium hydroxide in the same reagent would not have moved

explanation: This is the second test, and it settles it. The zinc hydroxide dissolves in ammonia where the aluminium hydroxide would not move, because zinc forms an ammine complex and aluminium has no such chemistry. Two white solids, indistinguishable by eye and identical in sodium hydroxide, separated cleanly by one reagent. Notice too that this solution is COLOURLESS, while the copper ammine from an earlier batch is deep blue. Zinc's d shell is completely full, so there is no room for the electron jump that gives transition metal complexes their colour — which is the usual reason for saying zinc is not really a transition metal at all.
source: Vogel's Textbook of Qualitative Inorganic Analysis 5th ed. — the zinc ammine complex; Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — d10 ions and colour

hazard.title: Chromium(VI) causes cancer
hazard.warning: Both the yellow chromate and the orange dichromate are chromium(VI), and chromium(VI) is a proven human carcinogen as well as being corrosive. The colour change is harmless to watch; the chemicals are not harmless to handle.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Gloves and eye protection, never by mouth pipette, and all chromium waste into the labelled heavy-metal container rather than the sink.

explanation: Yellow turns orange the moment acid is added, and the app already knew the reverse — add alkali to dichromate and the yellow comes back. Now both directions are here and they can be run against each other in one beaker. The essential point is what has NOT happened: the chromium is +6 before and +6 after, so despite how dramatic it looks this is not a redox reaction at all. Two chromate units have simply joined through a shared oxygen, the same way two acid molecules join to make an anhydride. Students lose marks on this every year by calling it a reduction.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — the chromate–dichromate equilibrium

effects.dissolves: the cream solid cleared away to nothing, which on a film is the unexposed silver being washed off

explanation: The cream precipitate dissolves away to nothing, and photography exists because of it. On a developed film the exposed silver has become the picture; the unexposed silver bromide is still sitting there, and left alone it would darken in daylight and destroy the image within minutes. Hypo removes it, and only hypo does the job this cleanly. Why thiosulfate and not, say, chloride? Because the donor atom is SULFUR, and soft donor atoms bind soft metal ions like silver far more strongly than hard donors do. That single principle — hard and soft, acids and bases — predicts this and a great deal else besides.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — hard and soft acids and bases, silver thiosulfate complexes

hazard.title: Chromium(VI) causes cancer
hazard.warning: Both the orange dichromate and the yellow chromate are chromium(VI), and chromium(VI) is a proven human carcinogen as well as being corrosive.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Gloves and eye protection, never by mouth pipette, and all chromium waste into the labelled heavy-metal container rather than the sink.

explanation: Orange back to yellow, and now the equilibrium really can be driven both ways in one beaker: add acid and it goes orange, add alkali and the yellow returns, as many times as you like. That is the whole character of an equilibrium — no reagent is used up in any permanent sense, and the colour simply reports where the balance currently sits. Keep hold of the point that survives all this switching: the chromium is +6 the entire time. What changes is how many chromate units are joined together, not the oxidation state of anything.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — the chromate–dichromate equilibrium

explanation: The first move of the systematic separation, and the logic behind the whole scheme is visible in it. Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to the unknown FIRST, before anything else, because only three cations in common use give an insoluble chloride — silver, lead and mercury(I). Whatever comes down here is one of those three; whatever stays in solution is not, and has been ruled out without being touched. Each later reagent narrows the field the same way. The curdy texture is characteristic, and so is the darkening in sunlight, which is the same light sensitivity that made photography possible.
source: Vogel's Textbook of Qualitative Inorganic Analysis 5th ed. — Group I, the chloride group

hazard.title: Lead is a cumulative poison
hazard.warning: Lead compounds are toxic and the body does not clear them — small exposures add up over years, and the damage to the nervous system is permanent. Children are affected at far lower levels than adults.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Gloves, no eating or drinking anywhere near the bench, wash hands properly afterwards, and all lead waste into the labelled heavy-metal container rather than the sink.

explanation: Lead gives a white precipitate with the very same reagent that just caught silver, so at this point the two are sitting in the same filter paper and cannot be told apart by eye. That is the normal state of an analysis after one test — a group identified, the individual not. The next two entries are how the group is taken apart, and they exploit a difference that has nothing to do with colour.
source: Vogel's Textbook of Qualitative Inorganic Analysis 5th ed. — Group I, the chloride group

effects.dissolves: the white solid went completely, leaving a clear solution that grows needle-shaped crystals again as it cools

explanation: Pour hot water on the mixed precipitate and the lead chloride dissolves and runs through the filter, while the silver chloride stays behind. Nothing has reacted — this is pure solubility, and it works because solubility is a property of a substance AT A TEMPERATURE rather than a fixed fact about it. Lead chloride's solubility climbs steeply with heat and silver chloride's hardly moves. Let the filtrate cool and needle-shaped crystals appear, which confirms the lead a second time. Note the app will not let this happen below about 80 °C, exactly as the real procedure insists.
source: Vogel's Textbook of Qualitative Inorganic Analysis 5th ed. — separation of lead from silver within Group I

explanation: The silver chloride sits there in the hot water unchanged, and that refusal is the other half of the separation. If both chlorides had dissolved, or neither had, the hot water would have told you nothing. It is worth being clear that a NEGATIVE result is a result: the solid still in the filter paper is now known not to be lead. To finish the identification, add ammonia — the app already knows that one, and the silver chloride dissolves in it as the diammine complex.
source: Vogel's Textbook of Qualitative Inorganic Analysis 5th ed. — separation of lead from silver within Group I

hazard.title: Hydrogen sulfide kills, and it stops smelling first
hazard.warning: Hydrogen sulfide is as toxic as hydrogen cyanide. The rotten-egg smell is not a reliable warning, because at dangerous concentrations it paralyses the sense of smell within minutes — so the smell going away is the worst sign, not a good one. People have died in drains and tanks for exactly this reason.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard, always, with the sash low. Never rely on smell to tell you the concentration. In a teaching laboratory thioacetamide, which releases the gas slowly in solution, is a much safer substitute and is now the usual choice.

explanation: A dense black precipitate the moment the gas goes through, and note the conditions: the solution is still ACIDIC from the hydrochloric acid added at the first step, and copper sulfide comes down anyway. It is so nearly insoluble that acid cannot hold it back. This is the group reagent for a whole family of metals — copper, lead, bismuth, cadmium, mercury, arsenic, antimony, tin — and the family is defined by precisely that property. The next entry is the same reagent on a metal that behaves the opposite way.
source: Vogel's Textbook of Qualitative Inorganic Analysis 5th ed. — Group II, the hydrogen sulfide group

explanation: Nothing. The same gas that threw down copper sulfide instantly leaves zinc completely alone, and this is the single most important negative result in the whole scheme. Zinc sulfide is far more soluble in acid than copper sulfide is, so in an acidic solution it simply cannot form — the acid pulls it apart as fast as it appears. That difference in solubility is what the entire separation of Group II from Group IV rests on. Make the solution alkaline and the zinc comes down at once, which is the next entry. Same metal, same reagent, opposite answer, and the only thing that changed was the pH.
source: Vogel's Textbook of Qualitative Inorganic Analysis 5th ed. — why Group II and Group IV are separated by pH

explanation: With the first two groups filtered off, ammonia is added and the hydroxides of iron, aluminium and chromium come down together — reddish brown for iron, white for aluminium, grey-green for chromium, so this group can often be read by colour alone. Ammonia is used rather than sodium hydroxide on purpose, and for two reasons: it is a weak base, so it will not go on to dissolve the amphoteric aluminium and chromium hydroxides the way excess sodium hydroxide would, and used with ammonium chloride it keeps magnesium in solution for a later group.
source: Vogel's Textbook of Qualitative Inorganic Analysis 5th ed. — Group III, the ammonia group

hazard.title: Hydrogen sulfide kills, and it stops smelling first
hazard.warning: Hydrogen sulfide is as toxic as hydrogen cyanide, and the rotten-egg smell disappears at dangerous concentrations because the gas paralyses the sense of smell. The smell fading is the worst sign, not a reassuring one.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard with the sash low, never judge the concentration by smell, and prefer thioacetamide in a teaching laboratory.

explanation: The same gas, the same zinc, and now a white precipitate — because the ammonia has made the solution alkaline and there is no longer enough acid to keep the sulfide dissolved. Put this beside the previous entry and the design of the scheme becomes obvious: hydrogen sulfide is used TWICE, once in acid and once in alkali, and the pH does the sorting. A white sulfide is also worth noticing in itself, since almost every other metal sulfide is black or brown, so the colour has half-identified the metal before any confirmatory test is run.
source: Vogel's Textbook of Qualitative Inorganic Analysis 5th ed. — Group IV, the ammoniacal hydrogen sulfide group

hazard.title: Soluble barium salts are poisonous
hazard.warning: Barium chloride and other soluble barium compounds are toxic if swallowed. The insoluble sulfate and carbonate are far less dangerous, which is why barium sulfate can be drunk as a medical X-ray meal while the chloride certainly cannot.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Gloves, no pipetting by mouth, and barium waste into the labelled heavy-metal container.

explanation: Barium, strontium and calcium come down together as their carbonates. The reagent is ammonium carbonate rather than sodium carbonate, and the substitution is deliberate — a weaker, more controllable source of carbonate that brings down only the least soluble ones. Once this group is filtered off, the only common cations left in the solution are magnesium, sodium, potassium and ammonium, which have no group reagent at all and are identified individually.
