source: Vogel's Textbook of Qualitative Inorganic Analysis 5th ed. — Group V, the ammonium carbonate group

explanation: The magnesium stays in solution, and it is meant to. Magnesium carbonate is not especially soluble, and adding SODIUM carbonate to the same solution would have brought it straight down — the app has that rule too, so the two can be run side by side. What keeps it dissolved here is that ammonium carbonate, used alongside the ammonium chloride already in the mixture, holds the carbonate concentration low enough to catch barium, strontium and calcium and no lower. This is the scheme at its most deliberate: the reagent was chosen for what it FAILS to precipitate, and that failure is what leaves magnesium behind for the last group.
source: Vogel's Textbook of Qualitative Inorganic Analysis 5th ed. — why magnesium is not in Group V

effects.dissolves: the magnesium ribbon slowly went, curl by curl, until none was left

hazard.title: Made and used in dry ether, which is extremely flammable
hazard.warning: Diethyl ether boils at 35 °C, its vapour is heavier than air and will creep along a bench to a flame several metres away, and the reaction itself gives out enough heat to boil it. The reagent formed is corrosive and reacts violently with water.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: No naked flames anywhere in the room. Heat only with a water bath, never a burner, and keep everything stoppered and dry.

explanation: The magnesium ribbon slowly disappears and the liquid turns cloudy — a Grignard reagent has formed. What has happened is a REVERSAL worth understanding rather than memorising. In bromoethane the carbon attached to the bromine is slightly positive, because bromine drags electrons towards itself; slide a magnesium atom in between and that same carbon becomes slightly NEGATIVE. A carbon that things attacked has become a carbon that attacks. That is why the next four entries can build carbon–carbon bonds, which nothing else in this app can do. Two practical notes the app cannot show: it is made in DRY ether, and the glassware must be dried in an oven first — the next entry is what happens if it is not.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — preparation of Grignard reagents

hazard.title: Immediate and vigorous
hazard.warning: The reaction is instant and gives out heat next to a solvent that boils at 35 °C and catches fire readily. A flask of Grignard reagent meeting a significant amount of water can boil over.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Quench deliberately and slowly, with cooling, and never let water reach the flask by accident — which means dry glassware and a drying tube from the start.

explanation: The most expensive mistake in a preparative organic laboratory, watched happening. All that careful work and the reagent is gone in seconds, giving nothing but ethane bubbling away — the bromoethane you started from, minus its bromine, and no use to anybody. The reason follows directly from the last entry: the carbon is now negatively charged, and a negatively charged carbon will take a hydrogen ion from ANY source it can reach. Water is the obvious one, but ethanol, an acid, even the moisture on undried glassware will do it. This is why the whole procedure insists on oven-dried apparatus and a drying tube.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — why Grignard reagents require anhydrous conditions

explanation: The first of three, and the three together are the whole point of Grignard chemistry. Count carbons: two went in as bromoethane, three came out. A carbon–carbon bond has been MADE, which is a different kind of achievement from swapping one group for another — it is how a bigger molecule gets built from smaller ones, and it is most of what synthesis is. Methanal is the special case, because its carbonyl carbon carries two hydrogens instead of one, so what comes out is a PRIMARY alcohol. Nothing else gives a primary alcohol this way.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — Grignard addition to carbonyls

explanation: The same reagent, an ordinary aldehyde this time, and the answer changes: a SECONDARY alcohol. The rule behind it is simple once seen. Whatever was already attached to the carbonyl carbon stays attached, and the Grignard adds one more group — so an aldehyde, which had one carbon group and one hydrogen, ends up with two carbon groups and one hydrogen. Count the groups on the carbon holding the OH and you have classified the alcohol. This is the middle case; the next entry is the third.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — Grignard addition to carbonyls

explanation: A ketone had two carbon groups on its carbonyl carbon already, so adding a third gives a TERTIARY alcohol — no hydrogen left on that carbon at all. The three entries together are the table worth learning: methanal gives primary, any other aldehyde gives secondary, a ketone gives tertiary. And notice how it connects backwards. A tertiary alcohol resists oxidation for exactly the reason a ketone did, and it is the same reason in both cases — there is no hydrogen on the important carbon to take off. The same structural fact keeps explaining different observations.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — Grignard addition to carbonyls

explanation: Carbon dioxide has a carbonyl group too, and the Grignard attacks it exactly as it attacked the aldehyde — nothing new is being learnt, the same reagent is simply pointed at a different carbonyl. What makes it worth its own entry is the result: a carboxylic acid one carbon LONGER than the halogenoalkane you began with, built by taking a carbon out of the air. Lengthening a chain by precisely one carbon is a genuinely awkward thing to do, and this is the standard answer. In the laboratory it is done by pouring the reagent onto solid carbon dioxide.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — carboxylation of Grignard reagents

explanation: The oxidation ladder run backwards. Ethanol was oxidised to ethanal with dichromate several batches ago; sodium borohydride puts the hydrogen back. Reduction and oxidation are the same ladder climbed in opposite directions, and knowing both means being able to move a molecule wherever you need it. The next two entries are about something more interesting than the direction, though — they are about what this reagent will REFUSE to do.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — reduction of carbonyl compounds

explanation: Nothing at all — and a reagent that fails is often more valuable than one that works. Sodium borohydride reduces aldehydes and ketones readily and will not touch a carboxylic acid, an ester or an amide. Now picture a molecule containing both a ketone and an ester, which is entirely ordinary in real synthesis. A reagent that reduced everything would leave you with a mess and no way back. This one reduces the ketone and leaves the ester untouched, and that ability to hit one group and spare another is called CHEMOSELECTIVITY. Choosing reagents for what they will not do is most of the craft of building a molecule.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — chemoselectivity of hydride reducing agents

hazard.title: Reacts violently with water, and with the acid itself
hazard.warning: Lithium aluminium hydride attacks anything with an acidic hydrogen, giving off hydrogen gas next to a flammable ether solvent. Adding it to an acid is vigorous before the reduction even begins, and quenching the excess afterwards is the step where accidents happen.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Dry ether, no flames, add the hydride slowly with cooling to the acid rather than the reverse, and quench the excess dropwise with great care behind a screen.

explanation: The carboxylic acid that sodium borohydride would not touch is reduced here without difficulty, all the way to the alcohol. Put the two side by side and the trade-off is plain: lithium aluminium hydride is far more powerful and correspondingly far less discriminating — it reduces aldehydes, ketones, esters, amides and acids alike — while sodium borohydride is weaker and therefore useful precisely because it is fussy. Neither is better. You pick the one whose reach matches the job, and if your molecule has only one reducible group you may as well use the powerful one.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — lithium aluminium hydride reductions

effects.precipitate: pale yellow crystals with a sharp antiseptic smell

explanation: The IODOFORM TEST, and it is unusually precise about what it detects. Pale yellow crystals with an antiseptic smell appear only if the molecule carries a CH₃CO— group attached to a carbon or a hydrogen, or an alcohol that oxidises to one — so a positive result names a specific FRAGMENT rather than a whole family the way Fehling's or Tollens' does. Propanone passes. Pentan-3-one, which is also a ketone, fails, because its carbonyl has an ethyl group on each side and no methyl. Note the arithmetic too: three iodine molecules go in and only one iodine atom ends up in the yellow solid.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — the haloform reaction; Vogel's Textbook of Practical Organic Chemistry 5th ed.

hazard.title: Benzene causes leukaemia, and the fumes are corrosive
hazard.warning: Benzene is a proven human carcinogen absorbed through skin as well as breathed in, chloromethane is toxic, and the reaction gives off steamy hydrogen chloride. Aluminium chloride reacts violently with any water it meets.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard, gloves, no skin contact with benzene at all. Where a reaction can be done in methylbenzene instead of benzene, it should be.

explanation: FRIEDEL–CRAFTS ALKYLATION: a carbon group put straight onto a benzene ring. The aluminium chloride does the essential work by being greedy for electrons — it pulls the chloride off chloromethane and leaves behind a fragment positive enough to attack a ring that normally protects its electrons fiercely. Worth knowing the catch, because it is why this reaction disappoints in practice: the methyl group it installs makes the ring MORE reactive than it was, so the product is attacked faster than the starting material and you end up with a mixture of multiply-substituted rings. The next entry is the way round that.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — Friedel–Crafts alkylation

hazard.title: Benzene causes leukaemia, and the fumes are corrosive
hazard.warning: Benzene is a proven human carcinogen absorbed through skin as well as breathed in. Ethanoyl chloride fumes in moist air and burns the airways, and the reaction produces more hydrogen chloride on top.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard, gloves, no skin contact with benzene. Keep everything dry, since both the acid chloride and the catalyst are destroyed by water.

explanation: FRIEDEL–CRAFTS ACYLATION, and it is the better reaction for a reason that is pure logic rather than chemistry-specific. The group installed here contains a carbonyl, which pulls electrons OUT of the ring — so the product is LESS reactive than the benzene it came from, and the reaction stops cleanly after one substitution instead of running away. Alkylation makes its product more reactive and cannot help going too far. When a chemist wants an alkyl group on a ring, the usual route is therefore to acylate first and reduce the carbonyl afterwards: two steps that work beat one step that does not.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — Friedel–Crafts acylation

hazard.title: Nitro compounds are toxic and the acid mixture is severely corrosive
hazard.warning: Nitrotoluenes are toxic and absorbed through skin. The nitrating mixture is concentrated acid and gets hot on mixing.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard, goggles and gloves, and cool the flask while the acids are mixed.

explanation: Nitration under conditions milder than benzene needs, and the product is a MIXTURE of two isomers — the nitro group has gone next to the methyl or opposite it, and essentially none has landed in between. This is ORTHO–PARA DIRECTING, and the reason is worth following rather than memorising: the methyl group pushes electrons into the ring, that extra density collects at the next-to and opposite positions, and an attacking electrophile goes where the electrons are. Two facts about the methyl group, one cause. It makes the ring react faster than benzene, and it decides where.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — ortho–para directing activators

hazard.title: Both nitro compounds are seriously toxic
hazard.warning: Nitrobenzene and dinitrobenzene are absorbed through skin, damage the blood's ability to carry oxygen, and the harm builds up with repeated small exposures. Hot concentrated nitrating acid is severely corrosive.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard, double gloves, and treat any skin contact as serious even when nothing is felt. Nitro waste goes in the labelled organic container.

explanation: The contrast this batch is built around. Toluene nitrated easily and gave the 2 and 4 positions; nitrobenzene needs HEATING to react at all, and the second nitro group lands at the 3 position — META. Both results come from the same cause read in opposite directions. The methyl group pushed electrons in, so the ring reacted faster and the ortho and para positions were richest; the nitro group pulls electrons OUT, so the ring reacts slower and those same ortho and para positions are drained hardest, leaving the meta position as the least bad option. The engine's demand for heat here is the deactivation made visible.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — meta-directing deactivators

effects.precipitate: a white solid, formed at once

hazard.title: Phenol burns skin without hurting at first
hazard.warning: Phenol causes severe burns and numbs the nerves as it does so, so the damage is often done before anything is felt. Bromine water is corrosive and its vapour attacks the eyes and lungs.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Gloves and eye protection, fume cupboard for the bromine, and wash any phenol contact off immediately with plenty of water whether or not it hurts.

explanation: Compare this directly with benzene. Benzene will not touch bromine water at all without iron(III) bromide to help — the app will tell you so if you try. Phenol needs no catalyst, no heat, and no waiting: a white precipitate appears instantly, and THREE bromines go on at once. That gap is the measure of how powerfully an OH group activates a ring, and the reason is the oxygen's lone pair being donated into it. The positions taken are 2, 4 and 6 — ortho and para, the same pattern the methyl group gave, because the same kind of donation is behind both.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — activation of benzene rings by hydroxyl

hazard.title: Picric acid is an explosive once it dries out
hazard.warning: 2,4,6-trinitrophenol is a powerful explosive when dry, and it becomes more sensitive still if it contacts metals and forms picrate salts. Laboratory stock is deliberately stored wet for this reason. A bottle found dried out is not something to move or open.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Leave a dried-out bottle alone, tell someone in charge, and let specialists deal with it. Keep any picric acid wet, away from metal fittings, and never let it dry in a stoppered container.

explanation: Phenol is so activated that nitration needs no sulfuric acid to help it and goes straight to THREE nitro groups. Then look at what those three groups do to the molecule they are on: picric acid is a genuinely strong acid, thousands of times stronger than phenol, because the nitro groups pull so hard on the ring that the O–H hydrogen leaves far more readily. That is the whole idea of substituent effects taken to its conclusion — the same OH group, in different company, behaves like a different class of compound. It is also a serious explosive, which is why it is kept wet.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — substituent effects on aromatic reactivity and acidity

effects.precipitate: black-brown manganese(IV) oxide, with white crystals of the acid appearing as it cools

explanation: The purple permanganate is discharged and brown solid appears — but read carefully what has been oxidised. The RING is untouched; only the methyl group hanging off it has been attacked, and it has been cut back to a COOH. The ring's stability is the point: those six electrons shared round it are held so well that hot permanganate, which tears an alkene apart, cannot get at them. Two more consequences worth knowing. However long the side chain, oxidation cuts it back to exactly one COOH — so propylbenzene gives benzoic acid too. And a ring with no side chain gives nothing at all, which is the next entry.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — side-chain oxidation of alkylbenzenes

explanation: The permanganate stays purple. Nothing happens, and after the last entry that should be striking rather than dull — the same reagent, hot, ate a methyl group off this very ring and cannot touch the ring itself. Set it beside the Baeyer test too, where an alkene decolourises permanganate in seconds at room temperature. Benzene has three formal double bonds and behaves like none: its electrons are spread evenly round the whole ring instead of being concentrated between pairs of carbons, and that spreading is what makes them unavailable. This negative result is the best evidence in the app that benzene is not simply cyclohexatriene.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — aromatic stability

effects.dissolves: the tin granules were eaten away as the mixture was boiled

hazard.title: Aniline is toxic and goes straight through skin
hazard.warning: Phenylamine is absorbed through unbroken skin, is toxic, and is a suspected carcinogen. It damages the blood's ability to carry oxygen and the effect of repeated small exposures accumulates. The starting material is no safer.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Gloves that aniline does not penetrate, fume cupboard, and treat any skin contact as a real exposure rather than a nuisance.

explanation: A nitro group reduced all the way to an amine, and with it the door into the whole of aromatic amine chemistry — dyes, drugs and the diazonium reactions that follow from here. The tin dissolves as it gives up its electrons. It is worth pausing on how completely the ring's character has flipped: nitrobenzene was DEACTIVATED and meta-directing, and aniline is one of the most activated rings there is, ortho–para directing and so eager to react that bromine water attacks it three times over with no catalyst. Same ring, opposite behaviour, and the only difference is what is hanging off it.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — reduction of nitroarenes to amines

effects.precipitate: a white solid, formed at once

hazard.title: Aniline is absorbed through skin
hazard.warning: Phenylamine is toxic and passes through unbroken skin, and bromine water is corrosive with a vapour that attacks the eyes and lungs.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Gloves and eye protection, and keep the bromine in a fume cupboard.

explanation: The same instant white precipitate phenol gave, three bromines at once and no catalyst — the nitrogen's lone pair floods the ring exactly as the oxygen's did. The batch now has a complete series to compare: benzene will not react without a halogen carrier, toluene reacts a little faster than benzene, phenol and aniline react instantly and three times over. One reagent, four rings, and the difference is entirely in what is attached. Being TOO reactive is a real problem, incidentally — putting a single bromine on aniline needs the amine tamed first, and that difficulty is a standard exam question.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — activation by amino groups

effects.dissolves: the orange powder went into solution, leaving a clear yellow liquid

hazard.title: Vanadium compounds are toxic and the dust is worse
hazard.warning: Vanadium(V) oxide is toxic and its dust irritates and damages the lungs. Vanadium solutions are toxic if swallowed and harmful to aquatic life.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Gloves and eye protection, avoid raising dust from the solid, and vanadium waste into the labelled heavy-metal container.

explanation: The starting point of the best colour demonstration in inorganic chemistry. Vanadium is unusual: it has FOUR oxidation states stable enough to sit in a beaker, and every one of them is a different colour, so a single tube can be walked down the whole series while you watch. This is the top of it, +5, and the next three entries take it down one step at a time. It is also the state vanadium(V) oxide is using when it catalyses the Contact process — the same compound met a long way back, now being examined rather than merely used.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — vanadium redox series

explanation: Yellow to blue, one electron at a time. Zinc is the reducing agent throughout this series, and the useful thing about it is that it is strong enough to keep going all the way down — add it in excess and the tube will pass through every colour in turn rather than stopping. The blue +4 state is the most stable of the four, which is why a vanadium solution left standing in air drifts back to this colour whatever you did to it.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — reduction of vanadium(V) by zinc

explanation: Blue to green, and something structural has happened alongside the colour. At +5 and +4 the vanadium was holding an oxygen — it was VO₂⁺ and then VO²⁺, never a bare metal ion. At +3 the charge has finally dropped far enough that it lets go, and what is in solution is a plain hydrated V³⁺. The colour change is the visible half of a change in what the ion actually IS. Note also that this green is easy to mistake for chromium(III)'s green, which is a fair warning that colour narrows a possibility rather than settling it.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — vanadium(IV) to vanadium(III)

explanation: Green to violet, and the end of the line — yellow, blue, green, violet, from one element in one tube. Vanadium(II) is where the series stops because it is now a powerful reducing agent itself, strong enough to pull oxygen out of the air and start climbing back up if the tube is left open. That is worth taking seriously rather than treating as a nuisance: an oxidation state can be easy to reach and hard to keep, and the two are almost the same statement seen from opposite ends.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — vanadium(II)

explanation: The same permanganate and the same iron(II) as the acidified reaction the app already knows — but with no acid added, and the manganese stops at +4 instead of falling to +2. This is the middle member of a set of three worth running together. In ACID, permanganate goes to colourless Mn²⁺. In NEUTRAL solution it stops here, as brown manganese(IV) oxide. In ALKALI it goes only as far as green manganate, which is the next entry. One oxidising agent, three different products, and the only variable is the pH.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — permanganate reduction products and pH

effects.precipitate: reddish brown iron(III) hydroxide in a dark green solution

explanation: Purple to dark green, and the manganese has moved only one step, from +7 to +6. Compare the three: acid takes it five steps down to +2, neutral takes it three steps to +4, alkali takes it one step to +6. The more hydrogen ions there are available, the further the reduction can go, because every one of those half-equations needs them. That is why a redox half-equation is written with H⁺ in it and why 'oxidising power' is not a fixed property of a reagent — it depends on the conditions you give it.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — manganate(VI) formation in alkali

hazard.title: Chromium(VI) causes cancer
hazard.warning: Potassium dichromate is a proven human carcinogen as well as corrosive. The chromium(III) produced is far less dangerous, but the starting material is handled with real care.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Gloves and eye protection, never mouth pipette, and all chromium waste into the labelled heavy-metal container.

explanation: Orange to green, and unlike the chromate–dichromate change from an earlier batch, THIS one really is a redox reaction — the chromium goes from +6 to +3, gaining three electrons. Worth holding the two side by side, because they look similar and are not. Adding alkali to dichromate turns it yellow and changes no oxidation state at all; adding zinc and acid turns it green and changes the chromium fundamentally. A colour change tells you something happened, never what.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — reduction of dichromate

explanation: Green to a bright blue that most students never see, because it will not last — chromium(II) is such a strong reducing agent that oxygen from the air takes it straight back to green chromium(III) within minutes. Keeping it means keeping air out. The parallel with vanadium(II) at the bottom of its own series is exact, and it is the general pattern: the lowest oxidation state a metal can be pushed into is usually the one most eager to give the electrons back.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — chromium(II) and air sensitivity

explanation: No blood red, no colour at all — and that is what makes the thiocyanate test worth running. Iron(III) gives an unmistakable deep red with thiocyanate; iron(II) gives nothing whatever. A test that reacted with both would tell you only that iron was present, which you probably already knew. This one separates the two oxidation states of the SAME element, which is a harder question and a more useful answer. It is also sensitive enough to catch iron(III) formed by a little iron(II) oxidising in air, so a faint pink in an old solution is worth noticing rather than ignoring.
source: Vogel's Textbook of Qualitative Inorganic Analysis 5th ed. — distinguishing iron(II) from iron(III)

explanation: The brown of the iodine fades to nothing, and this single reaction is the whole basis of iodometric analysis. Two thiosulfate ions each give up an electron and are joined together through their sulfurs into one tetrathionate ion — an exact two-to-one ratio, which is what makes it usable for measuring rather than merely observing. In practice the endpoint is sharpened by adding starch near the end, so the last trace of iodine shows as blue-black and its disappearance is unmistakable. Add the starch too early and it traps the iodine and ruins the reading.
source: Vogel's Textbook of Quantitative Chemical Analysis 6th ed. — iodometric titration

effects.dissolves: the white solid disappeared at once, giving a clear solution

hazard.title: Violently corrosive, and it gets very hot
hazard.warning: Sodium oxide reacts with water fast enough to spit, and what it makes is concentrated sodium hydroxide. Alkali in the eye causes permanent damage within seconds.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Goggles rather than spectacles, gloves, and add the solid to plenty of water in small amounts rather than the other way round.

explanation: The start of a walk across Period 3, and every entry after this is a comparison with it. Sodium oxide gives the most alkaline solution of any oxide in the period — pH 14 — and the reason is its BONDING. Sodium's pull on electrons is so much weaker than oxygen's that the electrons are handed over completely, leaving a lattice of ions; and a free oxide ion is one of the strongest bases there is. Follow the pH across the next five entries and it falls all the way to 1. Nothing about the oxygen changes; only the element it is joined to.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — Period 3 oxides and water

effects.precipitate: a faint white suspension that does not settle out

explanation: Still alkaline, but only pH 10 rather than 14 — the first step down. Magnesium oxide is still ionic, so it is still a base, but magnesium holds its two charges on a smaller ion and grips the oxide far more tightly than sodium did. Very little dissolves, and what does gives a weak alkali. This is the compound sold as milk of magnesia precisely because it is alkaline enough to neutralise stomach acid and too insoluble to do any harm beyond that.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — Period 3 oxides and water

explanation: Nothing. The powder sits there and the pH stays at 7, which is exactly the middle of the story. Aluminium oxide is at the point in the period where the bonding has stopped being properly ionic and has not yet become properly covalent, and the result is an oxide that will not behave as a base OR as an acid towards water. That does not make it unreactive — it makes it AMPHOTERIC, which the next two entries demonstrate by attacking it from both directions. An oxide that ignores water and dissolves in both acid and alkali is the signature of this part of the period.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — amphoteric oxides

effects.dissolves: the white powder went slowly into the hot alkali until the liquid ran clear

explanation: The oxide that ignored water dissolves in alkali, behaving as though it were an acid. Half the proof of amphoteric behaviour, and industrially the more important half: this is the Bayer process. Bauxite is aluminium oxide contaminated with iron oxide, hot alkali dissolves the aluminium and leaves the iron behind as red mud, and that single difference is how aluminium is purified at scale. Every drink can traces back to this reaction.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — amphoteric oxides and the Bayer process

effects.dissolves: the white powder went slowly into the hot acid until the liquid ran clear

explanation: And the same oxide dissolves in acid too, behaving as a base. Put this beside the previous entry and the case is closed: aluminium oxide is AMPHOTERIC, and the word means exactly this pair of results and nothing more mysterious. Worth noticing where the pH lands — 3, not 7. The aluminium ion left in solution is small and triply charged, and it pulls hydrogen ions off the water around it, so even the salt of a strong acid and this oxide comes out acidic.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — amphoteric oxides

explanation: Sand in water, and nothing happens — which is fortunate, given how much of the earth is made of both. Silicon dioxide IS an acidic oxide, so in principle it ought to react; the reason it does not is structural rather than chemical. It is one giant covalent network, and dissolving any of it means breaking strong silicon–oxygen bonds across the whole solid. Water cannot pay that price. The next entry shows what can, and how hard it has to try.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — giant covalent oxides

effects.dissolves: the sand went into the boiling alkali, leaving a thick syrupy liquid

hazard.title: Boiling concentrated alkali
hazard.warning: This needs hot concentrated sodium hydroxide, which is severely corrosive and attacks glass slowly as well as skin instantly.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Goggles, gloves, and a nickel or iron vessel rather than glass if the alkali is to be boiled for any length of time.

explanation: Silica does dissolve, but only in hot concentrated alkali and only slowly — proof that it is an acidic oxide, and proof at the same time of how weakly acidic. The comparison worth making is with phosphorus(V) oxide two places along, which reacts with cold water so violently it hisses. Both are acidic oxides of Period 3. The difference is entirely structural: one is a giant network that must be dismantled, the other is small separate molecules. Structure decides the RATE and the conditions; position in the period decides the acid-base character.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — silica and alkali

effects.dissolves: the white powder vanished into the water with a hiss

hazard.title: Reacts with water violently enough to spit
hazard.warning: Phosphorus(V) oxide takes up water so fast that the mixture hisses, steams and can throw itself out of the vessel. What it makes is a strong acid, and the solid itself burns skin on contact by pulling water out of it.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Goggles and gloves, add the solid in small portions to a large volume of cold water, and never the other way round.

explanation: The far end of the period, and the mirror image of where it started. Sodium oxide gave pH 14; this gives pH 1. The change is not gradual dithering but a clean consequence of one thing — how strongly the element on the other side of the oxygen pulls on the shared electrons. At the sodium end oxygen wins outright and takes them, leaving oxide ions that behave as a base. At the phosphorus end the electrons are shared, and what dissolves is a molecule that hands hydrogen ions to water instead. Ionic oxides are basic, covalent oxides are acidic, and Period 3 is that sentence made visible.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — Period 3 oxides and water

effects.dissolves: the crystals disappeared into the water and the pH did not move

explanation: Now the same walk again, this time with the CHLORIDES, and it starts as unremarkably as possible: salt dissolves and the pH stays at 7. That is the control the next two entries are measured against. Sodium chloride is fully ionic, and neither ion has any interest in the water beyond being surrounded by it — the sodium ion is big enough and its charge low enough that it does not pull hard on anything. Watch what happens when the metal ion gets smaller and more highly charged.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — Period 3 chlorides and water

effects.precipitate: a white solid of silica, formed instantly

hazard.title: Violent, with choking fumes of hydrogen chloride
hazard.warning: Silicon tetrachloride hydrolyses the moment it meets water — including the water vapour in the room, which is why the bottle fumes as soon as it is opened. The hydrogen chloride produced attacks the eyes and lungs.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard with the sash low, keep the bottle stoppered, and add it to water rather than water to it.

explanation: The other end of the chloride walk, and the contrast with salt could hardly be sharper: instead of dissolving quietly at pH 7, this hisses, throws down solid silica and fills the fume cupboard with hydrogen chloride at pH 1. The bonding has gone from ionic to covalent across the period, and a covalent chloride is hydrolysed by water rather than dissolved by it. There is a nice extra puzzle here too. Tetrachloromethane, the carbon version, does none of this — silicon is a bigger atom with empty d orbitals, so water can attach itself before any bond breaks, and carbon has no such opening.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — Period 3 chlorides and hydrolysis

hazard.title: Nitrites are toxic and give off nitrogen oxides
hazard.warning: Sodium nitrite is poisonous, and the nitrous acid it makes decomposes to brown nitrogen oxides if it is allowed to warm up. Those gases damage the lungs and the damage can be delayed by hours.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard, gloves, keep the mixture in ice throughout, and make only what is needed for the next few minutes.

explanation: Nitrous acid cannot be bought in a bottle, because it falls apart on standing and falls apart faster when warm. So it is made where it is needed, in the flask, from a stable salt and an acid — and the app insists on the cold, because a warm mixture destroys the reagent as fast as it appears. Generating an unstable reagent in place is an ordinary answer to instability rather than a special trick, and it is the first step of every diazotisation.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — generation of nitrous acid

hazard.title: Never isolate a diazonium salt, and never let it warm
hazard.warning: Benzenediazonium chloride decomposes above about 5 °C and the DRY solid is explosive. Attempting to filter one off and dry it has killed people. Aniline is also toxic and passes through skin.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Keep the flask in ice from start to finish, keep the salt in solution, and use it within minutes. There is no reason to isolate it and no safe way to do so in a teaching laboratory.

explanation: DIAZOTISATION, and the temperature is not a detail. Below 5 °C this works; a few degrees warmer and the product decomposes faster than it forms, which is why the app will not let it run out of the ice. What has been made is an amine with two nitrogens on the ring held by a bond that scarcely wants to exist — because nitrogen gas is such a stable thing to become that the group will leave in favour of almost anything. That reluctance is simultaneously why the compound is so useful and why it cannot be kept.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — diazotisation of aromatic amines

explanation: Take the flask out of the ice and this is what you lose it to. Bubbles of nitrogen rise, the diazonium salt is gone, and what is left is phenol — the same compound met several batches ago, arrived at by accident. This is the other half of the previous entry and the reason its temperature limit exists: the two rules together mean the ice bath is not advice a student can ignore, because ignoring it produces a visibly different result. Run deliberately with warm water, this is also a genuine preparation of a phenol from an amine.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — hydrolysis of diazonium salts

effects.precipitate: a bright orange solid, appearing the instant the two are mixed

hazard.title: Azo dyes stain everything, and some are carcinogenic
hazard.warning: The colour is the point, and it transfers readily to skin, clothing and bench. Several azo dyes made from aromatic amines are known carcinogens, and the alkaline solution used here is corrosive.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Gloves and a lab coat, and treat the dye as something not to get on you rather than something to admire on your fingers.

explanation: AZO COUPLING, and it is the most dramatic thing in this app — a colourless solution poured into another colourless solution gives an intense orange in an instant. The diazonium ion attacks the phenol ring, which is possible only because that ring is so heavily activated, and the alkali makes it more activated still by turning the phenol into a phenoxide. What results is two rings joined through an N=N bridge, making one continuous system of shared electrons long enough to absorb visible light. This reaction is why the modern chemical industry exists: the first synthetic dyes made from coal tar were worth more than the coal, and the companies founded to make them became the pharmaceutical industry.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — azo coupling

hazard.title: Aniline is absorbed through skin and azo dyes stain
hazard.warning: Phenylamine passes through unbroken skin and is toxic, and several azo dyes derived from aromatic amines are carcinogenic.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Gloves that aniline does not penetrate, and treat both the reagent and the dye as things to keep off you.

explanation: The same coupling with an amine instead of a phenol, and the dye comes out RED where the other came out orange. Nothing else about the molecule has changed — same two rings, same N=N bridge, one group swapped on the far end. That is dye design in a single comparison: the coupled system decides that there will be a colour, and the groups on the ends decide which colour, so a chemist tunes a shade by changing a substituent rather than starting over. Note also that no alkali is needed here; an amine is activating enough on its own.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — azo coupling with amines

explanation: Nothing at all, and after two instant dyes that should stop a student rather than disappoint them. A diazonium ion is a weak electrophile — much weaker than the nitronium ion that nitrates benzene — so it can only attack a ring that has been strongly activated first. Phenol and aniline qualify; plain benzene does not, and neither would methylbenzene. This is the activation series from an earlier batch reappearing as a hard limit rather than as a difference in rate. A reagent that couples only with activated rings is more useful than one that attacks everything, because it can be pointed.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — the diazonium ion as a weak electrophile

explanation: Iodine put onto a benzene ring, which cannot be done directly at all — iodine is too unreactive for the halogen carrier route that works for chlorine and bromine. Here it happens simply by adding potassium iodide, because the diazonium group leaves so readily that the iodide has only to be present. This is what makes diazonium salts worth the trouble of the ice bath: they are a doorway, and what walks through is whatever you put in the flask. Chloride, bromide, cyanide, water and hydroxide all work the same way.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — substitution of the diazonium group

equation: dye + cellulose → dye held in the fibre
explanation: The point of the whole batch, and worth being precise about: NO bond forms between the dye and the cloth. The dye molecule is flat and insoluble, cotton fibre is a tangle of cellulose chains, and the dye simply lodges in that tangle and is held there by the same weak attractions that hold anything to anything. That is why a direct dye like this one washes out over time, and why chemists later invented reactive dyes that do form a real bond to the fibre. Colour fastness is a separate problem from colour, and solving one does not solve the other.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — dyes and fibres

explanation: The cloth stays coloured in plain water, which is what a dye is for. It is worth knowing why this test is weaker than it looks, though: the dye is held only by weak attractions, so soap and repeated washing will eventually pull it out even though water alone does not. A single negative result at room temperature is evidence of fastness to water and evidence of nothing else — and the difference between those two statements is most of what testing a material carefully means.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — dye fastness

explanation: ADDITION POLYMERISATION, and the whole of it is one idea: the double bond opens, and each carbon uses the electrons it just freed to grab the next molecule along. Thousands of small molecules become one enormous one, and NOTHING is lost — count the atoms in the product and they are exactly the atoms that went in. That is what makes it addition rather than condensation. Note the heat given out: every double bond that opens releases energy, so an industrial reactor's real problem is cooling it, not warming it. The catalyst is not optional: without one this needs something like two thousand atmospheres, and with one it runs at ordinary pressure — which is why the app will not let it go until you add it.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — addition polymerisation

explanation: Ethane does not polymerise, and the reason is the same one that stopped it decolourising bromine water: it has no carbon-to-carbon DOUBLE bond. Addition polymerisation works by opening a double bond so each carbon is left with an electron to bond onwards with, and a molecule whose carbons are already fully bonded has nothing to open. This is why every addition polymer in this batch is made from an alkene and never from an alkane, and why the monomer is always drawn with that C=C showing.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — why addition polymerisation requires unsaturation

hazard.title: Chloroethene causes liver cancer
hazard.warning: The monomer is a proven human carcinogen — it causes a rare liver cancer, found among PVC plant workers in the 1970s. The finished polymer is not the danger; unreacted monomer is.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: This is industrial chemistry handled in closed systems for exactly this reason, not something to do in an open vessel. In a teaching laboratory it is demonstrated, not performed.

explanation: Exactly the same reaction as poly(ethene), with one hydrogen swapped for a chlorine on the monomer. That single change makes the finished plastic rigid rather than waxy, and it also makes it burn badly, giving off hydrogen chloride. Worth noticing that the polymer is harmless in a drainpipe while the monomer causes cancer — a polymer is a genuinely different substance from the thing it was made of, not simply a lot of it.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — addition polymers and their properties

explanation: The third time the same reaction, and by now the pattern should be doing the work: find the C=C, open it, join them up. What changes is only what was hanging off the double bond. Here it is a whole benzene ring, and once the chain is made those rings stick out along it and stop the chains packing neatly together — which is why polystyrene is hard and glassy where poly(ethene) is soft and waxy. The shape of a side group is a physical obstruction, and the properties of a plastic follow from it.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — side groups and polymer properties

explanation: The same reaction once more, now with every hydrogen replaced by fluorine — and the result is the most chemically inert plastic there is, the non-stick coating on a frying pan. The carbon–fluorine bond is the strongest single bond carbon forms with anything, and the fluorines wrap the chain in a sheath that keeps acids, alkalis and solvents from ever reaching the carbon backbone. It was discovered by accident in 1938, when a cylinder of the gas was found to have polymerised itself in storage.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — fluoropolymers

effects.precipitate: a tough off-white solid that can be drawn into a fibre

explanation: CONDENSATION polymerisation, and the contrast with the four reactions above is the point of the batch. Nothing here has a double bond to open. Instead each join throws out a small molecule — water — every time a link is made, so unlike an addition polymer the product does NOT contain all the atoms that went in. The link formed is an ordinary ester group, the same one made when ethanol met ethanoic acid; the only new idea is that both molecules have a reactive group at BOTH ends, so the joining never has to stop. This is the plastic drinks bottles are made of.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — polyesters

effects.precipitate: a milky white film at the boundary between the two liquids, which can be pulled out as a continuous thread

hazard.title: Corrosive reagents and hydrogen chloride fumes
hazard.warning: The acid chloride fumes in moist air and burns skin, the diamine is corrosive, and the reaction gives off hydrogen chloride as it goes. The thread being pulled out is wet with both reagents.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard, gloves and eye protection, and never touch the thread with bare hands — pull it with tongs or a glass rod and wash it thoroughly before handling.

explanation: The nylon rope trick, and it works at room temperature because an acid chloride is used instead of the acid. The two reagents sit in layers that do not mix, so the polymer forms only where they touch — and because it forms in a film at that boundary, it can be lifted out with tongs and pulled continuously, dragging fresh reagent to the interface as it goes. The link made is an AMIDE, the same C(=O)N bond that joins amino acids into a protein, which is why nylon is strong for the same reason silk is: chains hydrogen bonded tightly to their neighbours.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — interfacial polymerisation and polyamides

explanation: One monomer, not two — and glycine can do that because it is bifunctional all by itself, carrying an acid group at one end and an amine group at the other. Each join loses a water and makes an amide link, so this is condensation polymerisation exactly like the nylon two entries back, and the bond formed is the same bond. That is the point worth taking away: a protein is a condensation polymer, and nylon is a synthetic one built to the same plan. The difference is that a protein uses twenty different amino acids in a specific order, and that order is what makes one protein an enzyme and another a hair.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — peptide bond formation

effects.dissolves: the tough solid broke up and went into the hot alkali until nothing was left of it

hazard.title: Boiling concentrated alkali
hazard.warning: This needs hot concentrated sodium hydroxide, which is severely corrosive and does permanent damage to eyes within seconds.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Goggles rather than spectacles, gloves, and heat gently with anti-bumping granules rather than letting it boil hard.

explanation: The polyester comes apart again, back to the two monomers it was built from. It CAN be undone because the links along its chain are ester groups, and an ester is hydrolysed by hot alkali — exactly as ethyl ethanoate was several batches ago. This is chemical recycling as opposed to melting bottles down: the polymer is taken back to its starting materials and rebuilt from them, so the new bottle is as good as the first rather than slightly worse. Acidify the terephthalate afterwards and the dicarboxylic acid is recovered ready to use again.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — hydrolysis of polyesters and chemical recycling

explanation: Nothing, however long it is boiled — and after the previous entry that should land hard. Hot alkali took the polyester completely apart, and it cannot touch this at all. The reason is the chain itself: a polyester is joined by ester links, which are exactly the kind of bond alkali attacks, while poly(ethene) is one unbroken run of carbon–carbon and carbon–hydrogen bonds with no reactive group anywhere along it. It is simply a very long alkane, and alkanes are famously unreactive. That is why an addition polymer persists in the environment for centuries while a condensation polymer can be broken back down: not a difference in effort, a difference in what the chain is made of.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — why addition polymers resist degradation

effects.precipitate: soft pale amber lumps that clump together and can be lifted out

explanation: How rubber is actually harvested, and it is worth noticing that no polymerisation happens here at all — the tree already did that. The latex is tiny rubber particles held apart in water by a coat of protein carrying a charge, and like the clay in muddy water they repel each other and stay dispersed. Acid cancels that charge, the particles can finally touch, and they clump into a solid that is lifted out and rolled into sheets. The same idea as alum in a waterworks, done on a plantation with a bucket of acid.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — natural rubber processing

explanation: The latex stays milky and nothing settles, however long it stands — and that is what makes the previous entry a result rather than an inevitability. Diluting it changes nothing, because the problem was never concentration: every particle carries the same charge and pushes its neighbours away. Only something that cancels that charge will do it. Run this beside the acid tube and you have shown that coagulation needs a specific chemical cause, not merely time or stirring.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — colloid stability in latex

explanation: The synthetic route to the same rubber the tree makes, and it is addition polymerisation again — but with a monomer carrying TWO double bonds instead of one. Only one is used up joining the chain together. The other is left sitting in every single repeat unit, and the next four entries are all consequences of it: it is what bromine attacks, what sulfur uses to tie the chains together, and what ozone destroys. The catalyst matters more here than for poly(ethene), because it also controls which way round each unit joins, and getting that wrong gives a hard useless solid instead of rubber.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — diene polymerisation and stereochemistry

explanation: The orange-brown of the bromine water fades — the same test that told ethene from ethane several batches ago, now run on a lump of rubber. It works for the same reason and it proves the same thing: there are carbon-to-carbon double bonds here. That matters because it is easy to assume polymerisation must have used them all up. It did not, and the next entries depend entirely on the ones it left behind. A test learnt on a gas is not limited to gases.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — unsaturation in polydienes

effects.dissolves: the lump swelled, went sticky, and then disappeared into the solvent completely

hazard.title: Benzene causes leukaemia
hazard.warning: Benzene is a proven human carcinogen and is absorbed through skin as well as breathed in. A real workshop uses a less dangerous solvent for exactly this job.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard and gloves, and no skin contact at all. Where a job can be done in a safer solvent than benzene, it should be.

explanation: Raw rubber dissolves, and that single observation is the one this batch is built around — remember it, because the same test is run again two entries from now with the opposite result. It dissolves because its chains are separate objects: solvent works its way between them and floats them off one at a time. This is what bicycle puncture glue and rubber cement actually are. It is also why raw rubber is useless for a tyre, since anything that dissolves in petrol has no business near an engine.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — thermoplastic behaviour

equation: rubber + S₈ →(heat) rubber cross-linked by -S-S- bridges

effects.precipitate: a tough dark brown solid that springs back when pulled

hazard.title: Hot sulfur gives off choking sulfur dioxide
hazard.warning: Heating sulfur in air produces sulfur dioxide, which is sharply irritating to the eyes and lungs and dangerous to anyone asthmatic. Molten sulfur also burns skin badly.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard or strong ventilation, and heat gently — sulfur catches fire readily if it gets too hot.

explanation: VULCANISATION, and it is the whole reason rubber is a useful material rather than a curiosity. Short sulfur bridges reach across from one chain to the next and tie them together, using exactly the double bonds the bromine test just proved were there. What is remarkable is how little it takes: roughly one cross-link per few hundred units transforms a sticky solid that flows into something that snaps back every time. The chains can still uncoil when pulled, so it stretches — but they can no longer slide past each other and stay put, so it always returns. Charles Goodyear found it in 1839 by spilling the mixture on a stove.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — vulcanisation

explanation: Nothing dissolves. It swells a little and then stops, and after watching raw rubber vanish into the same solvent that should be startling. Same solvent, same test, same polymer chains — and the only difference is a scattering of sulfur bridges. Those bridges have tied every chain to its neighbours, so the solid is now ONE enormous molecule with no separate pieces for the solvent to carry away. Solvent still gets in between the chains, which is why it swells; there is simply nothing left that can leave. That is what THERMOSET means, and it is why a tyre survives a puddle of petrol.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — thermosets and solvent resistance

equation: rubber + O₃ → chains cut at the double bonds

effects.precipitate: a dull grey solid, cracked and brittle where it was soft

hazard.title: Ozone damages the lungs
hazard.warning: Ozone is toxic and attacks the airways at concentrations too low to smell reliably. Its sharp smell fades from awareness quickly, so smell is not a warning you can depend on.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard, and never rely on the smell to judge how much is present.

explanation: A rubber band left in a drawer for a year comes out grey, hard, and snaps instead of stretching. This is why. Ozone — present in ordinary air, and more of it in city air — attacks carbon-to-carbon double bonds and cuts them clean through, and cutting a long chain into short ones destroys the very thing that let it coil and uncoil. Now hold this next to the vulcanisation entry, because the same feature is doing both jobs: the leftover double bond is what lets sulfur make rubber useful, and it is the weak point that lets ozone destroy it. A structural feature is rarely only an advantage.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — ozonolysis and rubber perishing

equation: phenol + HCHO →(heat) cross-linked phenol–methanal network + H₂O

effects.precipitate: a hard dark reddish brown solid

hazard.title: Phenol burns without hurting, and methanal causes cancer
hazard.warning: Phenol causes severe burns and numbs the nerves as it does so, so damage is often done before anything is felt. Methanal is a carcinogen and its vapour attacks the eyes and airways.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Fume cupboard, gloves and eye protection throughout, and wash any phenol contact off at once with plenty of water whether or not it hurts.

explanation: The first fully synthetic plastic, made in 1907, and a thermoset reached by chemistry with nothing whatever in common with rubber's. This is CONDENSATION — a water molecule is thrown out at every join, and there is no double bond anywhere in it. What makes it set hard is that a phenol ring can be attacked at three positions, not two, so the growing structure branches in three directions instead of running in a line. There are no chains in the finished solid at all; it is a single continuous network.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — phenolic resins

explanation: Nothing again — and this is the entry that turns the batch into a general rule rather than a fact about rubber. Bakelite and vulcanised rubber have almost nothing in common: one is a condensation polymer of phenol and methanal built by branching in three directions, the other is an addition polymer of a diene tied together afterwards with sulfur. Different monomers, different mechanism, different bonds doing the joining. And both refuse the same solvent for the same reason, because in both cases everything is connected to everything else and there is no separate molecule left to dissolve. Cross-linking is what decides whether a plastic melts, dissolves and can be recycled — not what it is made of.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — thermoplastics and thermosets compared
